quotes.text: Notifications: only for things the player can act on (storage full, a character rested, an experiment finished, a heist against you). Players choose a daily reminder time, or none, and nothing is sent at night (see 20.2).
Off 22:00 to 08:00 by default
No win-back pressure. No escalating notifications, no "your islands miss you", no expiring comeback offers.
Contextual notifications open at 14.4% versus 4.19% for generic. But one weekly push causes about 10% of users to disable notifications and three to six causes about 40%.
This looks odd until you remember that a raid takes nothing: there is no harm to be protected from, and raids are anonymous while they happen.
The defender is notified afterwards and can watch the replay.

G34.also_needed: The clock must be settled under every option. The build stores a fixed offset with a default of 0 (db.mjs line 49). With that default a 13-to-15 in Brazil (UTC−3) gets pushes from 05:00 local, inside §20.2's "Never, 21:00 to 08:00", and a daylight-saving change moves a minor's night by an hour until the device reports again. Proposed rule: the device sends its IANA time zone (e.g. America/Sao_Paulo) with the push token and on every launch, the server works out the night from that zone, and no push goes to an account that has not reported one. That is one column and one check in notifications.mjs set() and due().

G29.question: Which telemetry definitions should the document adopt: what counts as a session, how long raw events are kept within 30 to 90 days, and whether the monthly survey is a monthly sample or a monthly ask?
G29.why_it_matters: The targets that open chapter 25 are read from these events, and nothing defines their unit. They are session length of 5 to 9 minutes, 3 to 6 sessions a day for active players, players still playing after 1, 7, 30 and 60 days, the "chore" share and the worth-your-time average. §25.3's crash-free share and absence warning are read from the same events. The build counts every sign-in as a session, so how many sessions one sitting makes depends on when the client signs in again, which it must do at least once an hour. The build also cannot report two of chapter 25's targets: 60-day retention and the chore share. §24's "monthly survey" and §25.4's "never more than once a quarter per player" disagree unless someone says how they fit together.
G29.today: server/src/telemetry.mjs and service.mjs. A "session" event is written on every POST /v1/session (service.mjs:145), and write() adds the player to first_seen on that event (telemetry.mjs:118-119). A token lasts 60 minutes (tokens.mjs:16, SESSION_MS). The server does not limit sign-ins. The client keeps the token only in memory (client/scripts/server_client.gd:9, 50) and must sign in again at least once an hour of continuous play. report() gives a raw session count and the crash-free share. It computes no session length: session_end seconds are stored but used only for the crash-free share (telemetry.mjs:244, 265). Raw events are kept 90 days (RAW_DAYS = facts.RAW_KEEP_DAYS[1]). A daily compact() then keeps only daily counts and, once a cohort is 31 days old, its day-1, day-7 and day-30 returns. The cohorts table has no day-60 column. The server accepts at most one survey per player per 90 days, counted from when it received the last one (SURVEY_GAP_MS, telemetry.mjs:32, 161-163). It has no sampler: who is asked is up to the client. The survey event is exactly 11 answers, each 1 to 7. The "worth" rating is 1 to 5, capped at 24 a day like session_end, and report() weighs each player once, by their own average. A batch holds at most 100 events dated no more than 7 days back (BATCH, LATE_MS). The pseudonym is an HMAC of the account. The client sends no telemetry yet.

options.label: Keep the build's readings
options.means: Everything as described under today, adopted as written. A session is a sign-in. Raw events are kept 90 days. The server accepts at most one survey per player per 90 days, and the client decides whom to ask. The survey is the 11-item inventory on a 7-point scale. The worth rating is 1 to 5, at most 24 a day, with each player counted once.
options.consequences: Session counts depend on client behaviour. A 70-minute sitting has to sign in at least twice, so it counts as two. Two short sittings count as one if the app keeps its in-memory token between them, and as two if it signs in again. That skews the 3 to 6 sessions a day target most directly. report() gives no session length, so the 5 to 9 minute target and the session count are not measured on one unit. Chapter 25's 60-day retention target (5%) and its chore share (10% or fewer) cannot be reported. Raw data kept is 90 days, the same as B and D.
options.numbers: 60-minute token (tokens.mjs:16). 90-day raw window (facts.json RAW_KEEP_DAYS [30, 90]). The 90-day survey gap (telemetry.mjs:32) allows at most about a third of players to answer in any month. The build has no sampler, so how many are asked is up to the client. If every eligible player is asked at 1,000 monthly players, 333 are asked and about 48 answer, using the document's one-in-seven response rate [182] (line 10093). The 95% margin on a 10% chore share is then ±8.5 points. At 10,000 players it is about 476 answers and ±2.7 points (recomputed in python).
options.doc_edit: §24 Analytics row: add "a session is a sign-in". §24.3: replace "30 to 90 days" with "90 days". §25.4: add that each player answers at most one survey in 90 days, and the eleven items are answered on a seven-point scale. Chapter 25's targets: drop 60-day retention and the chore share, or mark them not yet measured.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does

options.label: Device sessions, 90 days, sample with chore item
options.means: A session is the span from the app coming to the foreground to its session_end event, which the device is defined to send with its length in seconds (the client sends no telemetry yet). Sign-in only proves who the player is. Raw events are kept 90 days, as built. The monthly survey is a rotating sample: each month the client asks players not surveyed in the last 90 days. It is the 11 inventory items on 7 points plus one yes/no question, "does the game feel like a chore?", which chapter 25's targets read. Cohorts also record day-60 returns.
options.consequences: Session count and session length come from the same event. Chapter 25's 5 to 9 minutes and 3 to 6 sessions a day, §25.3's crash-free share and the absence bands all measure real play. All of chapter 25's retention, session and chore targets become reportable at soft launch. Survey rarity (§25.4) is unchanged. Data kept is the same as A.
options.numbers: Day-60 returns need raw events 61 days old, which fits inside a 90-day window. Survey sample sizes are the same as A: about 48 answers a month at 1,000 players and 476 at 10,000.
options.doc_edit: §24 Analytics row: define a session as foreground to session end, and say sign-in is not a session. §24.3: "90 days". §25.4: say the survey is a monthly sample, each player at most once a quarter, eleven items on a seven-point scale plus the chore question chapter 25 reads, which rides every survey and is not one of the extras rotated to small samples.
options.build_change: telemetry.mjs: add a session_start device event, or give session_end its start time. Count sessions from it in write()'s first_seen insert (telemetry.mjs:118-119), report(), cohort()/retention(), absence() and seasons.mjs:224. Have report() compute the median session length and sessions a day per active player from session_end seconds. Rename the sign-in event (for example to "sign_in"). The survey shape becomes 11 answers plus a chore flag. Add a day60 column to cohorts, and have compact() write a cohort at day 61 instead of day 31 (raw events at 90 days still cover it). The client must send the events and pick whom to survey.

options.label: Device sessions, raw events 30 days
options.means: The same session and survey as B, with raw events and replays kept only 30 days, the bottom of §24.3's range. Each cohort's day-1, 7, 30 and 60 figures are written as each falls due. This works because first_seen is kept apart from the raw events and each return day is recent when it is counted.
options.consequences: Least data kept, which fits §20.5's "collect only what's needed". Replays go after 30 days, because service.mjs:680 uses the same constant for replays. Disputes and "watch what a churned player did" (§24.3) then have a 30-day window. The once-a-quarter survey check reads a survey record that would be gone after 30 days, so it needs a separate last-surveyed date for each pseudonym.
options.numbers: RAW_KEEP_DAYS[0] = 30 (facts.json). The survey gap stays 90 days, which is longer than the 30-day window. The telemetry.mjs:32 comment relies on the reverse.
options.doc_edit: As B, but §24.3 says "30 days" for raw replays and logs.
options.build_change: As B. Also set RAW_DAYS to facts.RAW_KEEP_DAYS[0] and use it for replays (service.mjs:673, 680). Have compact() write each cohort column when due instead of all at once. Add a table of last-surveyed dates by pseudonym.

options.label: Monthly ask to every player
options.means: As B, but every player is offered the survey every month, and §25.4's once-a-quarter limit becomes once a month.
options.consequences: About three times the answers for the chore target. Surveys are no longer "short and rare": each player sees one about 12 times a year instead of 4. This contradicts §25.4 as written.
options.numbers: At 1,000 monthly players, about 143 answers (1,000 × 1/7) and ±4.9 points on a 10% share, against ±8.5 for a sample. At 10,000 players, 1,429 answers and ±1.6 points (recomputed in python).
options.doc_edit: §25.4: change "never more than once a quarter per player" to once a month. §24 and chapter 25: say the survey is asked of everyone monthly.
options.build_change: As B, plus SURVEY_GAP_MS about 30 days (telemetry.mjs:32).

recommendation.rationale: The 5 to 9 minute session and 3 to 6 sessions a day in chapter 25's targets are the unit the whole design is paced around, and counting sign-ins does not measure either. Under A, the 60-day and chore targets stay unreadable. Ninety days is inside §24.3's range and already carries the quarter rule. A rotating sample keeps surveys rare, as §25.4 asks.

quotes.text: Events for sessions, heists (outcome, laws crossed, crew), weaving, births and purchases, plus the "worth your time" rating and the monthly survey in 25.
Short retention. Raw replays and logs are kept 30 to 90 days, long enough for validation and analysis, then aggregated and discarded.
Surveys stay short and rare — the eleven-item experience inventory as the default, everything else rotated to small samples, never more than once a quarter per player.
Players who say the game feels like a chore (monthly survey)
Players still playing after 1, 7, 30 and 60 days
Sessions a day for active players

G29.also_needed: The wording of the chore question if B, C or D is chosen. The document does not give the inventory's scale: 7 points is the build's reading of the cited miniPXI, not the document's.

F43.question: When an account is deleted, which records stay under an id that leads to nobody, and do the player's Workshop islands stay playable?
F43.why_it_matters: §20.5 and §20.11 promise deletion. The ledger, Renown, snapshots and Workshop creations are built never to change (§24.12, §24.8, §19.11). Nothing says how the two meet, or what "anything collected" means for a player who turns out to be under 13. The store declarations (server/declarations.md) and the deletion button (D70) both depend on this answer, and the law carries per-violation penalties (§20.11).
F43.today: server/src/accounts.mjs deleteAccount(). Removed: the platform identity (replaced by "deleted:<id>"), equipped cosmetics, push token, reminder settings, telemetry batches and first_seen under the player's pseudonym, islands (out of matchmaking and target lists), notifications, friendships, invites and challenge links, and places in constellations and crews (a founder hands on). A raid already leased on one of their islands still settles for the raider (accounts.mjs:115-117). Workshop items are withdrawn, not deleted, so a remix still names its original. Kept under the opaque id: the ledger, Renown, heists, snapshots, leases, standings, season stars, purchases and more (server/privacy.json). Under 13 (erase()): also removed at once are replays they played, their island bytes unless shared, ratings, Workshop plays, ratings, completions and remixes, and open leases they held. Their name comes off Workshop reports. A raid leased on their island is refused (island_withdrawn, server/README.md), and target lists are remade without them. Ledger, Renown, season stars and purchases stay, severed. A ban survives only as the identity plus the day, in the bans table. §20.12's "unnamed derelict in the ruins" is not built.

options.label: Keep the build's reading
options.means: The person goes and the records stay, exactly as under today. Every deleted player's raid islands leave matchmaking. Their Workshop islands are withdrawn: no longer listed or playable, but still named as the original of any remix. An under-13 deletion also erases the replays, bytes, ratings, Workshop activity and open leases listed under today.
options.consequences: The ledger, Renown and snapshots stay append-only (§24.12, §24.8), and other players' histories, league standings and purchase records stay whole. Every deleted player's Workshop islands disappear from play, including ones others were remixing. This goes further than §20.12, where remaining as an unnamed derelict is the default and withdrawal happens only at the player's request.
options.numbers: server/privacy.json declares 39 tables and 236 columns. On deletion, 17 tables are severed, 7 erased, 6 erased only for under-13, and 9 left as they are: 7 not about a person, plus bans (the banned identity) and erasures (pending files). 22 tables are kept for good as records: the 17 severed tables and 5 of the under-13 ones (ratings and four Workshop tables). Recounted in python.
options.doc_edit: §20.12 "An account is deleted" row: list what is erased (identity, push token, telemetry, friendships, invites, links, group places, islands from matchmaking) and what is kept severed (ledger, Renown, heists, snapshots, season results, purchases). Replace "it may remain as an unnamed derelict in the ruins, or be withdrawn entirely at the player's request" with "its raid islands leave matchmaking and its Workshop islands are withdrawn". §20.11: define "anything collected" for under-13 as the build does.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does

options.label: Severed records, Workshop islands stay unless asked
options.means: Records as in A. A deleted player's raid islands leave matchmaking, as built; derelicts in the ruins are not built and are not part of this option. Their Workshop islands stay listed and playable with no creator shown. The deletion screen offers "withdraw my islands too", which does what A does. Under-13 islands are always withdrawn and erased as in A.
options.consequences: This matches §20.12's default, which treats the island as not personal data once the name is gone. Remixes and Workshop plays of a departed creator's islands continue, which protects §25.1's creation gate (10% of players remixing within 30 days). Players who leave lose their credit but not their work. The deletion flow gains one choice, on the device and on any web deletion page (G39), and the choice must be written into the deletion journal (F50) so a re-applied deletion keeps it.
options.numbers: Same table counts as A. workshop_items moves from "withdrawn" to "kept listed, creator severed" when the player does not ask.
options.doc_edit: §20.12: the same row as A, but the Workshop clause reads "Workshop islands stay playable without a name unless the player withdraws them at deletion; an under-13 player's are always withdrawn". §20.11 as A.
options.build_change: accounts.mjs: take a withdraw flag. Without it, skip the workshop_items UPDATE. workshop.mjs's listing must not show the severed creator. DELETE /v1/account (http.mjs) takes the flag, the deletion journal records it, and the client deletion screen (D70) shows it.

options.label: Under-13 depth for every deletion
options.means: Every deletion also erases what the build erases only for under-13 players: replays they played, island bytes unless shared, ratings, Workshop plays, ratings, completions and remixes, and open leases. Target lists are remade at once. Ledger, Renown, season stars and purchases stay severed.
options.consequences: Less of a departed player is kept. Replays of raids against their islands stop playing once the island bytes go. Workshop remixes lose a playable original. Each deletion regenerates every target list at once, not at the next 15-minute run.
options.numbers: The 6 tables marked erased-under-13 in privacy.json become erased for everyone. Replays go at deletion instead of after 90 days (RAW_KEEP_DAYS[1]).
options.doc_edit: §20.12: every deletion erases replays, island bytes, ratings and Workshop activity. The severed list shrinks to ledger, Renown, heists, snapshot rows, season records and purchases.
options.build_change: accounts.mjs: call erase() for every reason. privacy.json and declarations.md are regenerated (node server/src/privacy.mjs --write).

options.label: Erase the append-only records too
options.means: A deleted player's ledger rows, Renown, season stars, heists, standings and purchase rows are deleted, not severed.
options.consequences: Raiders' and defenders' histories lose heists they played. A constellation's combined Renown and league standings change after the fact, which is unfair to players who did nothing. The ledger stops being the single append-only record §24.12 and §24.13 rely on. Deleting purchase rows may break record-keeping that tax and store rules require, which needs legal advice.
options.numbers: Deletion needs the append-only triggers lifted on ledger (db.mjs:172-175), renown (289-292), season_stars (367-370) and purchases (415-418), plus rows deleted from heists, standings and season results. Snapshots (never-edited and never-deleted triggers at db.mjs:82-85) would need the same if they are included.
options.doc_edit: §24.12 and §24.8: drop "append-only" and "Never edited" for deletion. §19.11: qualify "never deleted or overwritten". §20.12: erase all records.
options.build_change: db.mjs: replace the triggers with a deletion-only path. accounts.mjs deletes the player's rows in those tables. seasons.mjs recomputes any open standings.

recommendation.rationale: Severing the records keeps the ledger and history fair to every other player and within one developer's scope. §20.12 itself says an island without its name is not personal data and may remain. Keeping Workshop islands playable unless the player withdraws them follows the document's own default and protects the remix gate. Under-13 deletion stays as deep as the build makes it.

quotes.text: Account and data deletion from inside the game.
A neutral age gate, no accounts below 13, and immediate deletion of anything collected from someone who turns out to be younger.
The island itself — terrain, guards, laws — is not personal data once the name is gone, so it may remain as an unnamed derelict in the ruins, or be withdrawn entirely at the player's request.
player creations are never deleted or overwritten (18.6)
Only then is the haul minted, into an append-only ledger

F43.also_needed: Legal advice on two points. First, whether severed records (an opaque id with no identity attached) meet erasure under GDPR. Second, what "anything collected" must cover for an under-13 player, including whether purchase and ledger rows may be kept. Also a build step under any option: an under-13 erasure must purge the erased island bundles from the edge cache, because http.mjs:326 serves them public and immutable for a year (see G38).

G32.question: When a store refunds a purchase after its Starglass was granted, what does the server take back, and can a Starglass balance go below zero?
G32.why_it_matters: A player can buy Starglass, spend it on a cosmetic or the premium track, then get a refund from Apple or Google. As built, they keep everything. Refunds already granted cannot be taken back until someone decides how. §20.2's monthly caps for minors also count every purchase, refunded or not. How fresh a sign-in proof must be is written nowhere in the document, only in stores.mjs.
G32.today: Proofs, all in server/src/stores.mjs. A Game Center signature must be within 5 minutes of the server clock (GAME_CENTER_FRESH_MS, :36, checked :234) under a pinned root. A Google ID token is accepted until its own exp plus 5 minutes of clock skew, and its iat may not be more than 5 minutes ahead (GOOGLE_SKEW_MS :304, :403-404); nothing bounds its age otherwise. A StoreKit 2 transaction must chain to its pinned root, match the app, be unrevoked and come from Production; Sandbox is accepted only if the operator sets RULEBORN_APPLE_SANDBOX=1 (stores.mjs:138-139, main.mjs:68). A Play purchase must be purchaseState 0, and is looked up and consumed before grant (googleapi.mjs). A purchase intent is held 15 minutes (shop.mjs:30), and the session token lasts 60 minutes (tokens.mjs:16). Refunds after a grant are not handled (D67): no App Store Server Notifications and no Play voided-purchases check. The balance is the sum of ledger rows (service.mjs:707). spendStarglass refuses when the balance is below the cost (service.mjs:727). It is called for cosmetics (shop.mjs:210) and the premium track (track.mjs:173). The schema does not stop a negative sum.

options.label: Keep the build's reading
options.means: The proofs are checked as under today. A refund after the grant changes nothing: the Starglass and anything bought with it stay. A grant is refused only when the store already reports the purchase at claim time (a revoked StoreKit transaction, or a Play purchase not in purchaseState 0).
options.consequences: Buy, spend, refund gives cosmetics and the premium track for free. Adults have no ceiling. Minors are limited only by their monthly cap. No power is at stake, because money buys only looks and a season pass (§22). This is the simplest option and needs nothing more.
options.numbers: Packs are €1, 5, 10, 20 and 50, booked at 100 to 5,000 hundredths of Starglass (shop.mjs PACKS; facts STARGLASS_PACKS_EUR [1, 50]). Caps are €25 a month for 13 to 15 and €50 for 16 to 17 (facts SPENDING_CAPS_EUR). A Game Center signature is accepted up to 5 minutes from the server clock. A Google ID token is accepted until its own expiry plus 5 minutes of skew, which is about an hour for tokens Google issues.
options.doc_edit: §24.8: add that a Game Center signature must be at most five minutes old, a Google ID token is accepted until its expiry with five minutes of clock skew, and a store receipt must be from Production. §22.1: add that a refund after purchase does not remove Starglass or anything bought with it.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does

options.label: Claw back in full; balance may go negative
options.means: When the store reports a refund, the server books a ledger row of minus the pack's Starglass. If the player already spent it, the balance goes below zero. Nothing can be bought with Starglass until the balance covers the cost again. Cosmetics and track tiers already bought are kept.
options.consequences: Refund abuse gains nothing lasting: the next purchase repays the debt first. No cosmetic is ever taken away, so no player loses an item they wear. The ledger stays append-only, because the refund is a new row (§24.12). A player refunded €50 of spent Starglass sees -50 and cannot spend Starglass, including on the premium track, until a purchase covers the debt and the cost. Earning it back is not a real way out: the free track gives 1 Starglass a season.
options.numbers: The worst case is -5,000 hundredths (one €50 pack) per refund. The existing check at service.mjs:727-728 already blocks spending while the balance is below the cost. The free track pays 25 hundredths at tiers 10, 20, 30 and 40 of 50 (track.mjs:52; facts SEASON_TIERS 50), so 100 hundredths a season; repaying -5,000 by play alone takes 50 eight-week seasons, about 7.7 years (recomputed).
options.doc_edit: §22.1: add "a refunded purchase is taken back from the Starglass balance, which may go below zero; nothing already bought is removed". §24.8: the proof freshness as in A.
options.build_change: A route for App Store Server Notifications v2 (REFUND and REVOKE) and a daily Play voided-purchases check (googleapi.mjs). Each books -price with reason "refund (22.1)" against the purchases row's account, once per transaction. shop.summary shows refunds. The operator configures the notification URL.

options.label: Claw back only what is unspent
options.means: On a refund, the server removes whatever of the pack's Starglass is still in the balance, down to zero. Anything already spent is written off.
options.consequences: The balance never goes negative. A player who spends first and refunds second keeps the cosmetic or track for free, so the abuse loop stays open, bounded only by minors' caps.
options.numbers: The claw-back is min(price, balance), between 0 and 5,000 hundredths.
options.doc_edit: §22.1: "a refund takes back unspent Starglass only". §24.8 as A.
options.build_change: As B, but book -min(price, balance).

options.label: Claw back and remove what it bought
options.means: As B, and anything bought with the refunded Starglass is taken back: cosmetics are removed from the collection and unequipped, and the premium track's claims are revoked.
options.consequences: This closes the abuse loop fully, but takes worn items away, which players experience as loss. Starglass is fungible, so tracing which purchase paid for which item needs a first-in-first-out rule over the ledger. That is more code for one developer.
options.numbers: Same as B for Starglass. The items removed depend on ledger order.
options.doc_edit: §22.1: "a refund removes the Starglass and anything it bought". §24.8 as A.
options.build_change: As B, plus FIFO tracing of Starglass spends to what they bought: cosmetics (removed from accounts.cosmetics and equipped, shop.mjs:210) and the premium track (track.mjs:173, its claims revoked).

recommendation.rationale: Money never buys power (§22), so the fairness question is only whether refunds become free items. A negative balance closes that loop with one append-only ledger row and never takes a worn item away. That is the smallest build for one developer, and it keeps §24.12's single-ledger rule.

quotes.text: No passwords. Platform identity is exchanged for a short-lived signed token.
Starglass, in packs from about €1 to €50
Family approval where set up; €25 a month cap
Money buys looks and a season pass. It never buys power, speed or chance.

G32.also_needed: Further decisions: whether a refunded purchase still counts against a minor's monthly cap (the build counts it); whether the proof windows are accepted (Game Center five minutes, Google token expiry plus five minutes); the Android identity question in D67 (Google account or Play Games player). Under §19.12 Starglass is also a gift wrapper, so the rule must say whose balance a refunded gift is taken from (the giver's, under B). And whether the server answers Apple's CONSUMPTION_REQUEST notifications with consumption information, which can lower refund approvals for spent Starglass under any option.

F50.question: How do a database restore and §24.6's table exports keep deletions made after they were taken, and where does the deletion log live?
F50.why_it_matters: §24.6 names two copies of the database: a point-in-time restore to any minute in the last 30 days, and "an export of every table kept elsewhere" for leaving the vendor. Restoring to a minute before a deletion brings back the identity, push token, telemetry and friendships, and removes the record that the deletion happened. An export made before a deletion holds the same data for as long as it is kept, and nothing limits its age. Both break §20.12's "backups included" promise, and nobody would know.
F50.today: server/src/accounts.mjs. Journal.append writes each deletion (account id, reason, time; nothing that names a person) to a local file with fsync before the deletion's transaction (accounts.mjs:44-70). reapplyDeletions() makes again every journalled deletion the database does not hold. main.mjs:169-176, the node:http server, runs it at every start, before the listener accepts sign-ins. The edge handler (http.mjs) never calls it. The journal path is RULEBORN_DELETIONS. By default it is server/.data/deletions.jsonl, the same directory as the database. privacy.json keeps the journal for good as §20.12's log. server/test/privacy.test.mjs restores a copy from before two deletions and checks both are made again. No table export is built.

options.label: Keep the build's reading
options.means: A write-ahead journal in a local file outside the database. Every entry the database does not show as deleted is made again at every server start, before anyone can sign in. The journal is kept for good as the log.
options.consequences: While the server runs as the Node process main.mjs starts, a restore can never bring a deleted player back and no step can be forgotten. The operator must point RULEBORN_DELETIONS away from the data directory, or a restore of that directory takes the journal with it. On the edge platform §24.1 names there is no durable local file and no start step, so the journal and the re-apply would have to move (see B and D). Exports are not covered.
options.numbers: About 79 bytes a journal line (24-hex account id, reason, millisecond time; recomputed with node). Each start reads the whole journal and makes one row read per entry ever journalled (accounts.mjs:245-246), and the count only grows. At 10,000 deletions, 500 starts a day would use the D1 free plan's 5 million daily row reads (5e6 / 1e4; line 13302). The paid plan's 25 billion a month absorbs it.
options.doc_edit: §20.12: add "each deletion is journalled outside the database before it is made, and every journalled deletion is made again whenever the server starts". §24.6 "Lost data" row: add that a restore is followed by re-making every journalled deletion, and that the journal is kept where a restore of the database does not reach.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does, on a server with its own disk. The deployment must set RULEBORN_DELETIONS outside server/.data/. It cannot run as built on §24.1's edge functions.

options.label: Journal in object storage, re-applied on restore
options.means: The same journal, stored in object storage, which the database's restore does not reach. It is re-applied as a fixed step of the restore procedure, of each deploy and of any export import, not at every start.
options.consequences: No per-start reads. A restore or import that skips the step brings deleted players back, so the procedure must be written down and followed, against §24.6's "no backup script to forget".
options.numbers: About 79 bytes a deletion, stored as one object each or appended, at the storage price in §24.1. No row reads except when a restore, deploy or import runs.
options.doc_edit: §24.6 "Lost data" row: "a restore or an import of an export is followed by re-making every deletion in the journal, which lives in object storage". §20.12 as A.
options.build_change: accounts.mjs Journal writes to the object store (store.mjs) instead of a local file. The reapply step moves from main.mjs start to an operator command, the deploy and the import. The default path inside server/.data/ is dropped.

options.label: Crypto-shredding
options.means: Every column that names a person (platform identity, push token, telemetry pseudonym key) is encrypted under a key for that account, and the keys are held outside the database. Deletion destroys the key. A restored or exported row is unreadable ciphertext.
options.consequences: A restore or an old export cannot resurrect a person even without re-applying anything. But every read of those columns decrypts, the key store needs its own backups that must not bring keys back, and lookups by identity need a keyed hash. This is the most work of the four for one developer. The journal is still needed as §20.12's log, though a restore no longer depends on it.
options.numbers: One key per account. The number of encrypted columns comes from privacy.json's user-id and identifier types.
options.doc_edit: §20.12: "personal fields are encrypted per account and deletion destroys the key, so no backup can restore them". §24.8: note the key store.
options.build_change: db.mjs, service.mjs, accounts.mjs, telemetry.mjs: encrypt and decrypt the personal columns, add a key store and keyed-hash identity lookup. The journal stays as the log.

options.label: Object-storage journal, re-applied at start within the restore window
options.means: The journal is written to object storage before each deletion. At every start the server re-makes only the entries from the last 31 days, the restore window plus a day, because a restore cannot bring back anything older. Table exports are kept no longer than 30 days, or the journal is applied whenever one is imported. The journal is kept for good as §20.12's log.
options.consequences: Automatic, with no step to forget (§24.6), and it runs on §24.1's edge platform. The per-start cost is bounded by one month's deletions, not all of them ever made. Both copies §24.6 keeps are covered.
options.numbers: Each start costs one row read per deletion in the last 31 days. For example, at 1,000 deletions a month and 500 starts a day, 500,000 row reads a day, a tenth of the D1 free plan's 5 million (line 13302). About 79 bytes a journal line, as A.
options.doc_edit: §20.12 as A. §24.6 "Lost data" row: "every deletion made in the last 31 days is re-made from the journal, which lives in object storage, whenever the server starts; table exports are kept at most 30 days".
options.build_change: accounts.mjs Journal writes to and reads from the object store (store.mjs). reapplyDeletions() filters entries by `at` to the last 31 days and runs at the edge handler's start as well as main.mjs's. An export job with a 30-day expiry, if exports are built.

recommendation.rationale: It keeps A's automatic re-apply, which holds even when nobody remembers a step, the reason §24.6 gives for automatic restore. A as built needs a local file, which the edge functions §24.1 names do not have, and its start-time cost grows with every deletion ever made. Bounding the re-apply to the 30-day restore window keeps each start to one month's deletions for a one-developer operation. A 30-day limit on exports makes "backups included" true for both copies §24.6 keeps.

quotes.text: Erasure completes within thirty days, backups included, with a log kept
Point-in-time restore to any minute in the last 30 days, automatically [199]. No backup script to forget
It is accepted deliberately, and bounded: plain SQL, no vendor-specific game logic, and an export of every table kept elsewhere.

F50.also_needed: Where the journal lives in the real deployment (which bucket or store, and who can write to it). Legal confirmation that keeping account ids in the log for good is acceptable. If F43 B is chosen, each journal entry must also record the player's withdraw choice.

G38.question: How long is something that names a player kept once it is closed (a sent notification, a used or lapsed friend invite, an expired challenge link, a superseded target list, a lapsed purchase intent, a lease that expired unplayed)?
G38.why_it_matters: §24.3 limits only raw replays and logs, and §20.5 says to collect only what is needed. Without a rule, closed records grow for good. The store declarations (declarations.md) must state how long each is kept. Target lists are public objects that name every candidate's account id.
G38.today: server/src/main.mjs runs tidy() at start and then daily (main.mjs:247-252), and the stored limits are declared in server/privacy.json. A sent notification is deleted 7 days after it was sent (notifications.mjs:29, SENT_KEEP_DAYS; the reminder check reads 3 days back). A used friend invite is deleted at the next daily tidy, an unused one after 7 days, and a challenge link after 7 days (friends.mjs:20-21, 118-124). Target lists are remade every 15 minutes and once at start (main.mjs:182-184, TARGET_LISTS_MS). Each band keeps its current list and the one before. The one before moves only when the band's list changes: a rebuild that produces the same bytes keeps the same hash and deletes nothing, so a superseded list is deleted when its band's list next changes, at least one rebuild later and with no upper limit in a quiet band (service.mjs:246-266). A band with no islands left loses both its lists (service.mjs:270-276). An under-13 deletion remakes the lists at once with no previous list (accounts.mjs:189). sweepLists() at start removes lists no band names (main.mjs:178). Lists are served through GET /v1/bundles with "public, max-age=31536000, immutable" (http.mjs:326), so an edge or device cache may hold a deleted list for up to a year. Purchase intents (held 15 minutes, shop.mjs:30) and leases are kept for good as records (privacy.json), including intents never redeemed and leases that expired still open; only an under-13 player's open leases are deleted. server/test/privacy.test.mjs runs each limit.

options.label: Keep the build's reading
options.means: A limit for each item, as under today: sent notifications 7 days, invites once used or at 7 days, challenge links at 7 days, target lists the current and previous per band. A daily job enforces the day limits, and each list rebuild enforces the list limit. Lapsed purchase intents and unplayed leases are kept for good as records.
options.consequences: Most closed things are gone within a week. A player's account id leaves the current list at the next rebuild, within 15 minutes of their island leaving the pool. The list before still names them until the band's list changes again: usually the next rebuild in a busy band, but never in a band where nothing changes. Cached copies may last a year. Lapsed intents and unplayed leases stay for good. Every new kind of closed record will need its own limit written down.
options.numbers: 7, 7 and 7 days (notifications.mjs:29, friends.mjs:20-21). Lists are rebuilt every 15 minutes (main.mjs:182). A superseded list lasts at origin from one rebuild (15 minutes) until its band next changes, with no upper limit (service.mjs:252-257). The cache header allows up to 365 days (http.mjs:326).
options.doc_edit: §20.5: add a short table of these limits, and say lapsed purchase intents and leases are kept as records. §24.8: say a band keeps its current and previous target list.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does

options.label: One rule: closed things go within 7 days
options.means: §20.5 gains one rule: anything that names a player and serves no purpose once closed is deleted within seven days of closing. A superseded target list counts as closed when the next one is made. Because a device may still fetch the list before, it is kept for one rebuild interval after it is superseded and then deleted, and every list is served with a cache life no longer than one rebuild interval. The build's notification, invite and link limits are instances of this rule.
options.consequences: Future features (clips, co-op invites, page requests) are covered without further edits. Target lists stop sitting in edge caches for a year: a list lasts at origin while current plus one rebuild interval, and a cached copy lasts at most one interval beyond that. A superseded list no longer waits for its band to change before it goes. Two closed things the build keeps for good fall under the rule and must be deleted: purchase intents that lapsed unredeemed and leases that expired unplayed.
options.numbers: 7 days is the longest existing lifetime of an invite or link (friends.mjs:20-21), and more than the 3-day reminder lookback (notifications.mjs:131). One rebuild interval is 15 minutes as built (TARGET_LISTS_MS, main.mjs:182), or an hour under G21 B, so target lists would get a max-age of 15 minutes, or an hour under G21 B, and a superseded list is deleted 15 minutes, or an hour, after it is superseded. An intent lapses 15 minutes after it is made (INTENT_MS, shop.mjs:30).
options.doc_edit: §20.5: add the one-line rule. §24.8: target lists are short-lived and not cached like island bundles; a band keeps its list before for one rebuild interval.
options.build_change: http.mjs: serve target lists with a max-age no longer than the rebuild interval (their own route, or a header chosen by object kind) instead of the one-year immutable header. service.targetLists(): record when the previous list was superseded (generated_at is rewritten at every rebuild, so it cannot serve) and delete it one interval later even if the band has not changed. A daily job deletes purchase intents unredeemed 7 days after they lapsed, and leases never played 7 days after they expired. privacy.json and declarations.md are regenerated. The other limits need no change.

options.label: Match §24.3: 30 days
options.means: Closed items are kept 30 days, the bottom of §24.3's raw-log window, so support can look a month back at a sent notification, an invite or a link.
options.consequences: About four times as long a trail naming each player. More rows count against the write-light budget, which is small at these sizes. It is harder to argue as "only what's needed" (§20.5).
options.numbers: 7 changes to 30 for SENT_KEEP_DAYS and for invite and link cleanup. Invites and links still expire for use at 7 days.
options.doc_edit: §20.5 or §24.3: "closed invitations, links and sent notifications are kept 30 days".
options.build_change: notifications.mjs:29 and friends.mjs expire() use 30 days. privacy.json and declarations.md are regenerated.

recommendation.rationale: One rule matches §20.5's "collect only what's needed", covers features the document has not built yet, and costs a single-developer project nothing to keep true. Applying it finds three gaps in the build: lapsed purchase intents and unplayed leases kept for good, target lists cached for a year where they should last no longer than one rebuild interval (an hour under G21 B), and a superseded list kept at origin until its band changes, which in a quiet band is never. All are small fixes.

quotes.text: Collect only what's needed to run the game; no advertising identifiers; analytics are pseudonymous.
Short retention. Raw replays and logs are kept 30 to 90 days, long enough for validation and analysis, then aggregated and discarded.
Candidate lists per difficulty band are generated periodically as static objects, so choosing a target costs a cached download rather than a database search.
Immutable, content-addressed island bundles on zero-egress object storage, cached at the edge for a year

G38.also_needed: A cache purge on deletion: a shorter max-age does not recall copies already cached. An under-13 erasure (F43) must purge the erased island bundles, and ideally the superseded lists, from the edge cache, because http.mjs:326 serves every object under /v1/bundles immutable for a year.

G39.question: What web route lets a player request deletion without the app, and how do they prove the account is theirs?
G39.why_it_matters: Google Play's Data safety form asks for a web link where a player can request deletion of their account and data without the app, for example after uninstalling it or losing the device. An app that creates accounts must give one. The document offers deletion only inside the game. The server stores no email or password, so a web request has nothing to match against unless the owner picks a proof.
G39.today: Nothing is built. server/privacy.json answers deletionUrl: null, and server/declarations.md:27 reads "a web link to request deletion: none yet (G39)". In-game deletion is DELETE /v1/account (http.mjs) and accounts.mjs deleteAccount(). The Android sign-in is "Sign in with Google". Its ID token is checked against RULEBORN_GOOGLE_CLIENT_IDS and the identity is gp:<sub> (stores.mjs:396-406). Game Center has no web sign-in.

options.label: Web page with Sign in with Google
options.means: A static page on the game's site explains what deletion removes and keeps. It offers Sign in with Google, which proves the same Google account the Android game uses, and shows the same choices as the in-game deletion screen (including F43's withdraw choice if chosen). The server then runs the same deleteAccount path at once, well inside §20.12's thirty days. iPhone players are told to delete from the game on any Apple device. Anyone who cannot is given the published contact address (§20.11), which has option C's weakness: nothing to prove the account is theirs.
options.consequences: The proof is automatic and adds no new personal data. The page costs nothing to host (static first, §24.4). It covers every Android player. It depends on the server knowing each Android player's Google account, which holds as built (gp:<sub>). If D67 moves Android to Play Games players, the Play Games sign-in must also request the openid scope and the server must store the Google sub, or the web proof must change.
options.numbers: Erasure within 30 days (§20.12). In practice it is immediate, the same as in-game deletion. The Google token check keeps its 5-minute skew (stores.mjs:304). Hosting cost €0.
options.doc_edit: §20.5: add "and from a web page, by signing in with the same Google account". §20.11: add a row for Google Play's web deletion link. §20.12: the thirty days apply to web requests too.
options.build_change: A static page. A web OAuth client id added to RULEBORN_GOOGLE_CLIENT_IDS. A route (for example POST /v1/account/delete with a Google ID token) that resolves gp:<sub> to the account and calls deleteAccount. privacy.json answers.deletionUrl set, and declarations.md regenerated.

options.label: Form with an in-game deletion code
options.means: The game's settings show a long account code. A web form takes that code and deletes the account it names, with a 30-day grace period during which signing in cancels the request.
options.consequences: It works for both platforms, but only for players who noted the code before losing the device, which is exactly the case the link exists for. Anyone who learns a code can delete that account, so the code must be secret and long. There is a new screen and a new secret to store.
options.numbers: 30-day grace, taken from §20.12's thirty days. The code needs at least 128 bits to resist guessing, more than the 96-bit account ids (12 random bytes, service.mjs:138) and on par with the 16-byte random intent ids (shop.mjs:103).
options.doc_edit: §20.5 and §20.11: a web form taking the account code, and deletion within thirty days unless the player signs in.
options.build_change: A code column (hashed) in accounts, a settings screen in the client, a form page and route, and a delayed deletion job.

options.label: Information page and a contact address
options.means: A page explains how to delete inside the game: signing in with the same platform account on any device reaches it. It gives a contact address for anyone who cannot. The developer handles emailed requests by hand within thirty days.
options.consequences: Almost no build. But the server holds no email, so an emailed request cannot be proved against an account. Google may not accept a page that sends players back into the app. Each request costs the one developer time.
options.numbers: 30 days to answer (§20.12). No new stored data.
options.doc_edit: §20.11: a row for the web link as an information page with a contact address.
options.build_change: A static page. privacy.json answers.deletionUrl set, and declarations.md regenerated.

options.label: Keep the build: in-game only
options.means: No web route, as built. Deletion is offered only inside the game.
options.consequences: Google Play's Data safety form cannot be completed truthfully, so the game cannot ship on Google Play. Android is 81 to 95% of target markets (§24).
options.numbers: declarations.md:27 stays "none yet". The 81 to 95% Android share comes from §24's Reference device row.
options.doc_edit: §20.11 would have to say the launch is iOS-only.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does

recommendation.rationale: Signing in with Google proves ownership with the identity the server already verifies, collects nothing new, and deletes at once through the tested in-game path. It suits a one-developer, static-first build (§24.4) and keeps §20.12's thirty-day promise without manual work. It covers the Android players Google's rule is about.

quotes.text: Account and data deletion from inside the game.
published contact details, and account deletion inside the app [194]
Ongoing moderation, in-app reporting and blocking, a terms-of-use gate, and a truthful data-safety declaration
Erasure completes within thirty days, backups included, with a log kept

G39.also_needed: Two further answers. D67's answer on whether the Android identity is the Google account or a Play Games player; A depends on it. A check of Google Play's current deletion-link policy text, including whether an information page (C) is accepted.

G23.question: Where the launch law sheets in §7.7 stop short, should the rules be the simulation's readings as built, those readings with Delay's promised weakness made real, or rules you write yourself?
G23.why_it_matters: The server re-simulates every heist (§24.7), so whatever sim/ reads is the rule every replay is judged by, whatever the sheet says. Under those readings two sheets promise things the build does not do. Delay's weakness, "Your own guards react late too", is not a rule anywhere, so Delay has no weakness. Bounce's raider and defender lines need a character to rebound, which happens only under Pinball (Frictionless + Bounce), so Bounce alone just returns half a blow to whoever strikes a ward. Aurora's single two-row band lights a tile only 12.5 to 16.7% of the time, so in practice it mostly halves vision, like Glowing dark. Density is a separate case: §11.2 makes four ruleborn small, but sim/ plays roles, not ruleborn, so nobody is small in the build. That is a gap in the build, not a reading to adopt.
G23.today: sim/ applies all 24 launch laws, and each reading sits beside its code in sim/src/lib.rs. Frictionless: only the crew slides; guards do not; a Halt stops a slide and the grid edge ends it (slide_on, line 3217). Bounce: a character rebounds only while sliding, so only under Pinball, off every wall. Bounce alone just returns 50% of a blow on a ward to the striker, and a Warden absorbs both (around lines 2361-2365). Density: the Warden counts as large and every other role as standard, so nobody is small, because the simulation's crew and guards are roles, not ruleborn (by_size, line 256; Role::size, line 280). Delay: holds ward effects only (queue `delayed`, lines 2480-2484 and 2555-2559); guards react on time. Aurora: one band 2 rows deep (heist.rs AURORA_BAND_ROWS) sweeps north to south once per 10 s period (in_band, line 1463). Chain lightning: jumps to the nearest standing member of the struck side within 3 tiles; a jump never jumps again, and hits on structures do not jump (chain_from, line 2775). Static: a charge builds after 5 tiles; a touch means the same or an adjacent tile; the stun lands on the nearest body, ally or not (static_touches, line 1693). Echoes: the return happens at once, where the character fell, after its loot has dropped. Soul swap: once per character; the one swapping takes none of the blow; only a hit sets it off (soul_swap, line 2669). Thorns: a touch means standing on or beside a wall or a live Thorn Hedge, costing 5% of full health once a second, and the Vault and pylons do not count (thorns, line 2832). Each reading is held by a test in sim/src/tests.rs. sim/ plays every law at its tier I figure.

options.label: Keep the build's readings
options.means: Every reading above becomes the written rule, exactly as sim/ plays it now: guards react on time under Delay, a character rebounds only under Pinball, and Aurora is one 2-row band per sweep. Density's small band stays as §11.2 writes it and waits on the build.
options.consequences: Nothing changes in play. Delay keeps no weakness for its defender unless you write a new one. Bounce alone stays a defender's law, and its raider and defender lines have to describe Pinball. Aurora stays a near-constant halving of guard sight. Whichever option you pick, Density plays as a Warden-only rule (+30% health, -20% speed) until sim/ carries each character's ruleborn.
options.numbers: Aurora lit share = band rows / (grid rows + band rows), from in_band's formula: 2/12 = 16.7% at realm level 1 (10 rows), 2/14 = 14.3% at level 3, 2/16 = 12.5% at level 5 (recomputed in python3). Density at tier I: large +30% health and -20% speed, small -20% health and +25% speed (sim/src/laws_table.rs line 76: 13/10, 4/5, 4/5, 5/4).
options.doc_edit: §7.7: add each reading to its law's Tier I cell (Frictionless, Bounce, Delay, Aurora, Chain lightning, Static, Echoes, Soul swap, Thorns). Replace Delay's 'Its weakness' line, which the rule would make false, and rewrite Bounce's raider and defender lines to name Pinball, the only way a character rebounds. Leave Density's raider and defender lines as written: §11.2's small ruleborn make them true once the build carries each character's ruleborn. §7.4 regenerates from §7.7.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does

options.label: Keep readings; Delay slows guards too
options.means: As A, but under Delay a guard's change of state (Suspicious, Investigating, Alerted) also lands 3 s after its suspicion crosses the threshold (3.5 s and 4 s at tiers II and III once the build carries tiers), so the weakness the sheet names becomes a rule.
options.consequences: Delay cuts both ways, as §7.7 requires. A seen crew gets a 3-second window before guards respond, and a defender who takes Delay pays for late wards with late guards. Hourkeeper's resist and the Clear-headed trait (§11.2, §11.3) then protect against something real. Everything else is as A, including Bounce's rewritten lines and Density waiting on the build.
options.numbers: 3 s at tier I (sim/src/laws_table.rs line 85: EffectDelaySeconds 3/1); 3.5 s and 4 s at tiers II and III (§7.7 Delay sheet), which the build does not play yet because it has no law tiers.
options.doc_edit: §7.7: as A for the other eight laws, including rewriting Bounce's raider and defender lines to name Pinball. Delay's Tier I cell becomes 'Wards and abilities take effect, and guards change state, 3 seconds after they are triggered', and its weakness line stays as written. §7.4 regenerates.
options.build_change: sim/src/lib.rs: queue guard state transitions under EffectDelaySeconds the way `delayed` already queues ward effects; add a test in sim/src/tests.rs; regenerate the golden replays for Delay realms.

options.label: Write each sheet's rule yourself
options.means: You write the missing rule for each of the nine sheets in the sheet's own words, for example whether guards slide, whether a character rebounds outside Pinball, how deep and how many Aurora bands there are, and what counts as a touch. The build then changes to match.
options.consequences: The sheets say exactly what you intend. Every reading you replace means a code change, a new test and a golden-replay refresh, and until then the server keeps enforcing the readings. Density still waits on the build carrying ruleborn.
options.numbers: none until written
options.doc_edit: §7.7: your rule in each of the nine Tier I cells, plus any weakness, raider or defender line your rule makes false; §7.4 regenerates.
options.build_change: sim/src/lib.rs and sim/src/heist.rs: change each replaced reading and the test that holds it (sim/src/tests.rs); refresh golden replays.

recommendation.rationale: §7.7 sets the bar: a law without a weakness does not ship, and under the build's reading Delay has none. The document already assumes Delay slows reactions: its sheet says 'Characters flinch a beat late', and §11.3's Clear-headed trait and Hourkeeper's resist make characters immune to it, which only matters if Delay does more than hold wards. B keeps the other tested readings, costs one queued state change, and makes the written sheet match the rule the server replays.

quotes.text: A law that cannot be used by both sides is not finished, and a law without a weakness is not shipped.
Your own guards react late too.
Characters flinch a beat late; effects land after a pause.
Clear-headed: immune to Spores and Delay.
Bands of light sweep the realm every 10 seconds. Inside a band everyone can be seen from twice as far; between bands, vision halves.
Ricochet past a guard you cannot out-fight.
Your Breakers become slow targets.
Under 2.0 heads is small, 2.0 to 2.5 standard, above 2.5 large. That yields 4 small, 10 standard and 4 large, and every large one is a Warden, which is why Density reads as a Warden rule in play.

G23.also_needed: Under any option: Density's weakness line, 'Your Breakers become slow targets.', is false by §11.2's own roster (no Breaker is large, and Emberling, a Breaker, is small); it should read 'Your Wardens become slow targets.' sim/ must carry each crew member's and guard's ruleborn Size (§11.2) in place of Role::size (sim/src/lib.rs line 280) before Density's small band plays. Also decide whether Bounce alone passes §7.7's both-sides test, since without Frictionless it only returns half a blow to whoever strikes a ward. Under A, a new weakness sentence for Delay.

G24.question: Should §7.3's Structure regrowth row be split into a heal-while-standing row and a regrow-after row, and when two laws set a regrow time, which time applies?
G24.why_it_matters: One row holds three different rules: Regrowth heals what is still standing, Bloom and Crystal growth regrow broken things after a set time, and Tidemark rolls broken things back to a mark. That is the fault §7.3 says version 2 of the sheet fixed for Drain and for Healing and regrowth: one name for several rules. §7.3's combining rule covers only multipliers and on/off values, so a time has no stated way to combine. The build therefore multiplies times like any other number: Bloom and Crystal growth together regrow a hedge after 51.2 s, far slower than either law alone.
G24.today: sim/ keeps the heal as Param::StructureRegrowth (Regrowth, 2%/s) and the timer as Param::RegrowSeconds (Bloom 10 s, Crystal growth 8 s; sim/src/laws_table.rs lines 74, 97, 103). The timer applies only to broken Thorn Hedges (sim/src/lib.rs, around lines 2378-2402), so Crystal growth's walls and its 'clear crystal' do not exist. Every value, times included, combines by multiplication in Sheet::apply (sim/src/lib.rs line 115, called from refresh_sheet, line 1181). refresh_sheet applies the standing laws in weave order, the order the island lists them (World::weave, line 830), with no layer or school sort. A scratch test on a copy of sim/ that wove both laws gave 1,536 ticks = 51.2 s: 10 s × 8 s, each cut a fifth by the Bloom harmony both laws carry (harmonised, line 152). Tidemark is `simulated: false` (laws_table.rs line 88). Crystal growth and Tidemark are not launch laws, so at launch only Bloom sets a time.

options.label: Keep the build's reading
options.means: One row in the document, two parameters in sim/. Regrow times multiply like every other value, the regrow timer applies to Thorn Hedges only, and Tidemark stays unbuilt.
options.consequences: Nothing changes at launch, because Bloom is the only launch law with a timer. Once Crystal growth ships, weaving it beside Bloom makes hedges regrow much later, not sooner. The row still names one parameter for two subjects.
options.numbers: Bloom + Crystal growth = 51.2 s (1,536 ticks), from a scratch test on a copy of sim/ (8 s × 6.4 s after the harmony). Bloom alone 10 s (300 ticks), Crystal growth alone 8 s (240 ticks).
options.doc_edit: §7.3: name the row's two subjects in 'Changed by', and add that times multiply like multipliers.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does

options.label: Split the row; shortest time wins
options.means: Rule sheet version 3 with twenty-three parameters. 'Structure healing' covers Regrowth (standing buildings, wards and guards heal N% a second). 'Structure regrowth' covers Bloom (cut hedges), Crystal growth (broken walls and hedges, as clear crystal) and Tidemark (return to the mark). When several laws set a regrow time, the shortest one applies, and what comes back is that law's.
options.consequences: Weaving two regrowth laws makes regrowth faster, as a player would expect. With Bloom and Crystal growth together, a cut hedge comes back after 8 s as Crystal growth's clear crystal, not after 10 s as a hedge; whether clear crystal blocks sight is not written (its sheet calls it cover), so that needs a line. The sheet's version changes before anything has shipped, so no pinned island or replay is affected, the same reason version 2's split was free. Launch play does not change.
options.numbers: Bloom + Crystal growth at tier I: shortest of 10 s and 8 s = 8 s, or 6.4 s after the Bloom harmony's fifth-shorter wait (8 × 4/5, harmonised() in sim/src/lib.rs line 152). Parameter count goes from 22 to 23 (§7.3).
options.doc_edit: §7.3: split the row into two named rows. Change 'twenty-two' to 'twenty-three' in the section's opening sentence ('The sheet has exactly twenty-two parameters') and in the closing paragraph, and 'version 2' to 'version 3'. Add 'a regrow time takes the shortest value applied' to the combining sentence. §7.7's Regrowth Effect kind cell ('Parameter: changes Structure regrowth') names 'Structure healing'; §7.4 regenerates.
options.build_change: sim/src/lib.rs: in Sheet::apply, combine RegrowSeconds by minimum rather than product, and have the regrown tile take the winning law's kind. Leave TouchStunSeconds, EffectDelaySeconds and LightBandSeconds as they are: they share era.rs's Kind::Time (sim/src/era.rs line 145), but each has one setter and they are durations or waits, not regrow times. Rename StructureRegrowth to match and bump the rules version. content_gate.py and design_facts follow the new count.

options.label: Split the row; last time applied wins
options.means: As B, but a regrow time takes the last value applied, like an on/off rule, in §7.3's order: layer first (Era, Grand Law, crown laws, realm laws), then school order Motion, Matter, Time, Energy, Life, Spirit.
options.consequences: The outcome depends on application order, which players never see. Within one layer Crystal growth (Matter) applies before Bloom (Life), so Bloom's slower time wins; a crown-law Bloom beside a realm-law Crystal growth would lose to it.
options.numbers: Bloom + Crystal growth in one layer at tier I: Bloom's 10 s, or 8 s after the Bloom harmony (10 × 4/5).
options.doc_edit: §7.3: as B, with 'a regrow time takes the last value applied' in the combining sentence.
options.build_change: sim/src/lib.rs: for RegrowSeconds, Sheet::apply overwrites rather than multiplies, and refresh_sheet must first sort the standing laws by §7.3's layer and school order (it applies them in weave order today); bump the rules version.

options.label: No split; add the time rule only
options.means: Keep version 2's twenty-two parameters and one Structure regrowth row, but reword the row to name both subjects and add 'a regrow time takes the shortest value applied' to §7.3.
options.consequences: The two-laws-set-a-time case gets an answer, but the row still carries one name for several rules, the fault version 2 fixed for Drain and for Healing and regrowth.
options.numbers: Bloom + Crystal growth: 8 s at tier I, 6.4 s with the harmony (as B).
options.doc_edit: §7.3: reword the Structure regrowth row's default and 'Changed by', and add the time rule to the combining sentence.
options.build_change: sim/src/lib.rs: minimum rule for RegrowSeconds only in Sheet::apply; no rename.

recommendation.rationale: §7.3 split Drain and Healing and regrowth for exactly this reason, and says a split is free while nothing has shipped; after launch it would pin replays. 'Shortest time wins' is the rule a player can predict by reading the two sheets, while layer and school order are invisible to them. The build already keeps two parameters, so the code change is one combining rule on one parameter.

quotes.text: None; broken things stay broken
Multipliers multiply; on/off rules take the last value applied
Version 1 had twenty; Drain and Healing and regrowth each named one parameter for two subjects
A law that needs a twenty-third parameter is a design decision that makes version 3, never a content addition
Broken walls and hedges regrow as clear crystal after 8 seconds.
Buildings, wards and guards heal 2% of their health each second.

G24.also_needed: Whether Tidemark's return-to-mark sits in the regrow-after row or needs its own wording, since it is a periodic rollback rather than a timer; and, under B or D, whether Crystal growth's clear crystal blocks sight.

G36.question: Should §18.3's eras run as the build runs them (a fixed rotation, on every heist against a universe but not in the Workshop, with 'stronger' read line by line), or with one of these changes?
G36.why_it_matters: §18.3 lists eight rules and says 'each week', but not which week gets which, which heists an era covers, or what 'stronger' means for a time, a rate or a multiplier. The server stamps the era on every lease and refuses a replay that names another era, so these readings decide real outcomes. A player who can't predict or read the week's rule can't plan for it.
G36.today: server/src/eras.mjs runs the eight in content/eras.json order, one a week counted from the first season's first day (eraAt, line 27, called with this.seasons.first at server/src/service.mjs line 403), so each comes once per eight-week season while seasons run back to back. server/src/service.mjs issue() (around lines 401-448) stamps the week's era on every lease against a universe: raid, echo, Trace, friendly heist and challenge. A replay naming another era is refused (line 499). The Workshop leases with clockTicks(0) and no era (server/src/workshop.mjs lines 117, 246). sim/src/era.rs: Wildgrowth reads 'stronger' by line kind (line(), line 91): a time comes 25% sooner, a rate is 25% larger, a multiplier moves 25% further from 1, and on/off rules are unchanged. The era applies before any harmony. The Long Night cuts guard sight by 30%; Heavy Stars switches off Half gravity's line (suspends, line 83); Static Storm scales the Static Coil's shock ×1.5 (ward_strength, line 117); Echoing Skies is one Revival source at 40%, and the highest N applies. The cost halves of Heavy Stars and High Tide are not built (D69). sim/ has no law tiers: every woven law plays its tier I figure.

options.label: Keep the build's reading
options.means: Order: Heavy Stars, The Long Night, High Tide, Wildgrowth, Echoing Skies, Static Storm, Glass Moon, Quiet Week, one a week counted from the first season's first day (server/src/eras.mjs eraAt), so each season gets all eight in that order as long as seasons run back to back. G25.question: Should §8's thirty-six launch combination rows take the simulation's readings as their rules, take them with 'stronger' read as the value itself 25% larger, or be rewritten by you row by row?
G25.why_it_matters: Almost every harmony, dissonance, resonance and chord row is one sentence, so sim/ had to decide what each actually does, and the server replays by those decisions (§24.7). Some rows can't be played in full with the launch laws. The Veil harmony strengthens nothing, because neither launch Veil law (Delay, Soul swap) is an illusion. Glow can only lengthen Aurora's band. Lantern festival's lanterns need Soul lanterns, which is not a launch law. Cracked gardens' Essence has no amount. The 'stronger' reading alone moves crew speed by nearly half again, and decides whether the Weight harmony slows more or less (see numbers).
G25.today: sim/src/combos.rs works out which of the 8 harmonies, 4 dissonances, 12 launch resonances and 12 chords sound, from the standing pylons, every tick. sim/src/lib.rs applies them. Harmonies: HARMONY_KINDS (line 130) and harmonised() (line 152) read '25% stronger' as the law's change made a quarter larger (a multiplier's distance from 1 × 1.25; a wait 1/5 shorter), applied once to a parameter however many shared notes or laws cover it, and only to the harmonising laws' own parameters. Glow adds 2 rows to Aurora's band (heist.rs GLOW_HARMONY_ROWS); Hush treats the one being looked at as a tile further off; Veil does nothing. Figures the document does not give are listed in sim/content_gate.py READINGS (line 76): déjà vu within 60 s of the clash first sounding, Wildfire burn 5%/s, Deep sleep muffles footsteps by one step, Fair lights every 20 s, Quicksand opens 3 pits, a pit holds for 1 s. Other readings: Storm grid jumps 3 times, each from the last; Lantern festival plays only its return; Mirage shows a character on the tile it just left; Clockwork fires every triggered ward. Each is held by a test in sim/src/tests.rs.

F33.question: Should the Lantern Glare stay a realm-wide alarm, be limited to one per realm, send every guard to investigate its tile, or Alert only the guards within 4 m of it?
F33.why_it_matters: §5.2 budgets defence by counting wards, but a Glare Alerts every guard in the realm within about half a second, so a Keeper's budget really buys Glares. On the harness (n=400), one Glare lifts realm 3's hold from 36.2% to 78.0%, and two shut it at 99.0%. One ward that decides the outcome breaks §13.2's rule that no single layer does. The register asks for the check to run over the kits a Keeper can build, not only over the generator's mix, and that check also shows ward count is not a steady dial for any kind: three Gravity Wells hold 88.8% and six hold 32.0%.
F33.today: sim/src/lib.rs: when a Glare fires, fire_ward (lines 2600-2606) sets revealed_until and reveal_spot, and every guard gets the near-zone fill toward the Glare's tile for 5 s (lines 1249-1257; heist.rs GLARE_REVEAL_TICKS, GLARE_BLIND_TICKS). At 67 a tick that is Alerted in about 15 ticks. The ordinary alarm already spreads by distance: guards within guard::SPREAD_METRES (4, guard.rs line 68), scaled by the sheet's AlarmRange factor, are told half a second later (lib.rs lines 3048-3067; the Whispers law sets that range to 999). The Glare ignores this reach. The harness sets every guard to ALERTED (tools/heist_harness/sim.py line 608). The generator hands out kinds in turn: Snare, Well, Glare (tools/heist_harness/island.py around lines 344-356). A Glare counts as one ward against §5.2's limits (sim/src/island.rs WARD_LIMITS line 62, checked at line 414). tools/heist_harness/test_harness.py:827 test_one_lantern_glare_outweighs_a_realm_of_other_wards pins the current behaviour.

The standard error is about ±2.5 points near 50% and ±1.5 near 90%. Seven cells were re-run and matched exactly. Results: no wards 36.2%; 1 Glare 78.0%; 2 Glares 99.0%; 3 Glares 99.8%; the generator's six (§5.2's budget) 89.5%. Snare/Well kits of 1 to 6 wards: 36.2, 41.0, 64.2, 63.2, 50.0 and 34.2%; 8 of them 95.8%. Wells alone, 1 to 6: 30.2, 30.5, 88.8, 75.8, 72.5 and 32.0%. recommendation.rationale: All three judges agreed on the goal: under §13.2's rule that no single layer decides outcomes, the Glare must stop being a realm-wide switch, and A and B fail that test (one Glare plus others holds 94-95%). Two judges (player experience, scope) chose the investigate-at-tile rule with a one-per-realm cap. Their case rested on the earlier draft's figures, and each named, as its main risk, that sending guards to the tile might prove stronger than the proxy that was measured. The balance judge measured the rule as written, and I reproduced it at n=400: 1 Glare holds 91.8%, and with the cap 1 Glare + 3 others holds 100%. So that dissent carries: limiting the Glare's reach to §12.17's own 4 m alarm spread is the only tested rule that turns it into a dial (1 to 3 Glares 68-77%, the generator's six 89.5% to 61.2%). It also meets what the other two judges wanted: a readable, recoverable setback, no stacking switch, and a one-line change that reuses existing spread code with no editor rule. Confidence is medium: 6 Glares still sit about 5 points above the best Glare-free kit (3 Wells, 88.8%), the harness crews know where every ward is, the 8 m alarm-4 reach is unmeasured, and realm 3 stays above its band under every option.

panel.reasoning:
From the player's side, the Glare as built (option A) is a hidden tile that ends the raid. Line 5880 of the design document says the Glare is "Hidden until revealed or fired", and it triggers when a crew member comes within 2 tiles. It then Alerts every guard in the realm within about half a second. So a crew that did not scout that one tile finds out the raid is over, not that it made a mistake it could recover from. That goes against §12.17 ("nothing here is random: a player who scouts an island can predict exactly what will happen") and §1.2's pillar ("Heists are won by reading an island's rules and finding a way through, not by bigger stats."). In a 20-minute session, an instant loss the player could not see coming is the most frustrating kind of failure.

Option B stops a Keeper stacking Glares, but it keeps the switch. On the harness, one Glare plus five other wards holds realm 3 at 96.2%, so one hidden tile still decides the raid, and the player feels exactly what they feel under A.

Option C turns the Glare into the kind of setback a heist story is made of. The alarm goes off, every guard walks to that spot, and a crew that moves during the 2-second blind can slip away or use the empty rooms. §12.17's Investigating row ("Walks to the spot and searches nearby for ten seconds, twenty from alarm level 3") already spells out behaviour the player can read. But C alone still lets a Keeper stack Glares: 2 hold 88.8% and 3 hold 97.5%. A realm full of Glares plays as a minefield, a raid ended by an early misstep, and it breaks §13.2's "If one layer decides outcomes, the others are decoration."

Option D keeps C's readable, recoverable effect and caps the Glare at one per realm. The cap is also something the player can scout: a crew knows there is at most one Glare to find. The best kit with a Glare (71.2%) lands level with the best kit without one (67.5%), inside the ±5-point standard error at n=80, so a Keeper chooses among kinds rather than buying one decisive ward. That fits §1.2's rule that wins come from reading an island's rules, not from bigger stats.

The build cost is small: one effect line in sim/src/lib.rs, one check in island.rs check(), and the matching lines in the harness. That suits one-developer scope.

Confidence is medium. The harness crews know where every ward is. The investigate rule that was measured is weaker than the one written. And realm 3 still holds above its 30–45% band under every option, so §5.2's ward counts need re-measuring over the kits a Keeper can build.

I re-ran the harness at n=400 a cell, with the brief's settings: realm 3, 2 posts, one geometry band, three realms crossed, crack noise off, competent crew, defensive laws, v3.4 rules. The standard error is about ±2.5 points near 50% and ±1.5 near 90%. The harness copy and driver are in scratchpad/brief/f33j (run.py; GLARE_MODE in tools/heist_harness/sim.py).

1. The draft's C and D rest on the wrong measurement. The rule they describe, with every guard going to Investigating and walking to the Glare's tile, makes the Glare stronger than today:
- 1 Glare holds 91.8% against the build reading's 78.0%.
- 2 Glares hold 99.8%.
- The generator's six hold 99.2% against 89.5%.
- D's best allowed kit (1 Glare + 3 others) holds 100%.
The draft's 57.5% came from raising suspicion to 600 with no destination, which is not what §12.17's Investigating does ("Walks to the spot"). What makes a Glare decisive is pointing every guard in the realm at a tile on the crew's route. Whether they arrive Alerted or Investigating barely matters. 2. B barely helps. One Glare plus 3 others holds 94.5%, and one plus 5 others holds 94.2%, so the jump from a single Glare stays.
