- Alerting only guards within 4 m of the tile: 1 Glare 68.2%, 2 Glares 75.2%, 3 Glares 76.5%.
- The generator's six fall from 89.5% to 61.2%.
- Each extra Glare now adds a few points instead of shutting the realm.
It reuses a distance rule §12.17 already states for the alarm. This fits "If one layer decides outcomes, the others are decoration" (§13.2), and it is a one-line build change for a one-developer scope. Investigate-at-tile within 4 m is not a dial either: 87.0%, 93.8%, 97.8%.

4. The draft's "best Glare-free kit 67.5%" is wrong. Three Gravity Wells hold 88.8%, while Well kits of 1 to 6 hold 30.2, 30.5, 88.8, 75.8, 72.5 and 32.0%. Snare/Well alternating kits of 1 to 6 hold 36.2, 41.0, 64.2, 63.2, 50.0 and 34.2%, 8 of them hold 95.8%, and no wards at all hold 36.2%. So ward count is not a dial for any kind. §13.2's check (31.5) must run over the kits a Keeper can build whatever is chosen here, and realm 3's six-ward, two-post budget likely needs resetting. One Glare stays above the 30-45% band under every option.

5. The build is probably stronger than any harness figure above. The harness sets ALERTED for one tick, and the Alert lapses after the 0.5 s state floor. sim/src/lib.rs (lines 1249-1257 and 2600-2606) instead applies near-zone fill for 5 s with every guard's interest on the Glare's tile. That is closer to the 91.8% rule than to the 78.0% one.

6. Economy: none of the options changes a Starlight price, and a ward costs 350 Starlight at level 1 (tools/economy_model data). The cost-three version in B and D saves at most 700 Starlight a realm, which is negligible. The economy model assumes raids succeed 60% of the time from day 31 (data.heist_success_rate). The build reading's generator mix at realm 3 (89.5% hold, about 10% success) breaks that assumption much more than the reach dial does (61.2% hold).

Confidence: medium. It is high that C and D as written go the wrong way. It is lower that 4 m is the right radius, because 1-post realms and the 8 m at alarm 4 were not measured, and the harness crews know where every ward is.

panel.variant: D, built on what the sim already has so the change stays small. (1) The Glare's effect is the heard event cracking already uses (§12.17: "It is a heard event, not a suspicion increment, because suspicion added below 600 drains before it can move an unaware guard."). In sim/src/lib.rs fire_ward (about lines 2600-2606), call the existing lure(gi, w.tile) for every awake guard, which sets interest to the tile and enters Investigating, or set guard.heard = Some(w.tile) as the crack path at line 1915 does. Then delete the revealed_until/reveal_spot near-zone fill at lines 1249-1257. In the harness, set g.heard to the Glare's tile and raise suspicion to at least INVESTIGATING (sim.py line 608). The harness already holds Investigating until the heard spot has been searched (sim.py about lines 522-529). This also measures the rule as described, with guards sent to the tile, which the brief's C/D numbers do not yet do. (2) The budget rule is one line in sim/src/island.rs check(): a Glare takes three ward places, so wards.len() + 2*glares must stay within WARD_LIMITS[level], and a second Glare is refused with a new Problem. The client editor's ward counter shows places used, not wards. Regenerate golden replays with the existing `cargo run --bin golden -- --write`, because Island::example() places a LanternGlare at (3, 9). Rewrite the harness test test_one_lantern_glare_outweighs_a_realm_of_other_wards (tools/heist_harness/test_harness.py:827) into the kit check: best Glare kit minus best Glare-free kit, within the standard error.
panel.reasoning:
From the scope and build-risk side, D is the only option that makes the ward budget something one developer can test, and it is cheap because both halves reuse code that already exists and is tested. Options A and B leave a switch in place: one Glare plus other wards holds 96.2% at realm 3. The §13.2 build-blocking check can then only pass by special-casing kits, so the rule that "no single layer decides outcomes" can't be tested at all. C by itself still lets a Keeper stack Glares (2 at 88.8%, 3 at 97.5%, against 67.5% for the best Glare-free kit). That means the kit check stays red, and every change to ward counts later has to be re-measured against an all-Glare kit. D brings the best Glare kit within realm 3's six places (71.2%) level with the best Glare-free kit (67.5%), inside the ±5-point standard error at n=80. That turns the §5.2 count back into a dial the harness can check with one assertion.

The engine cost is small. The sim already has the Investigating-at-a-tile verb: lure() at lib.rs about line 1168, used by illusions and sounds, and the heard path at line 1915, used by cracking. The Glare becomes one more caller of it, and a special reveal/near-zone branch goes away, so the perception code gets a little smaller. The budget rule adds one weighted count and one new Problem next to the existing TooManyWards check in island.rs line 414. The editor and the server (which runs the same sim check) pick it up without new systems. The content cost is none: no new art, no new ward, and the §10.3 row keeps its shape.

It also fits the document's goals. The Glare becomes a readable event at a known tile, matching §1.2's "Heists are won by reading an island's rules and finding a way through, not by bigger stats." and §13.2's "If one layer decides outcomes, the others are decoration." Confidence is medium. The harness crews know where every ward is. The investigate rule has only been measured in its weaker form (suspicion raised, guards not sent to the tile). Realm 3 stays above its 30-45% band. Realms with eight places (1, 2, 5) allow one Glare plus five others and have not been measured under D.

The build currently answers in two different ways: the economy model uses level 1, while the sim and server let the island's own level byte decide.

G26.question: Which figures should §18.6, §18.7 and §20.12 give the Workshop: the server's current ones, the same rules with a larger quota and larger word lists, or no figures in the document at all?
G26.why_it_matters: The server already enforces the Workshop with figures the document never gives: how many islands a player may publish, how much storage they get, what 'cleared' means, what a player can report an island for, what a completion 'spike' is, and whether a remix earns its original anything. If nobody decides, the build's guesses become the game's rules without review. Four of them are visible to players: the name pool, the slot count, the report reasons, and the quota when it refuses a publish. Two of the build's figures hurt the creators §18.7 rewards: the quota is a lifetime cap, and the name pool produces duplicate names almost at once.
G26.today: server/src/workshop.mjs holds each reading as a named constant with a test (server/test/workshop.test.mjs). Names: an adjective plus a noun from server/src/words.json, 16 × 16 = 256 names, in English and Brazilian Portuguese (workshop.mjs:22, 76-81). Constellation names come from the same lists (social.mjs found(), lines 58-61; D63). Slots: SLOTS = 5, and BUILDER_SLOTS = 3 more for §18.7's Builder, so 8 (workshop.mjs:30-31). Quota: QUOTA_BYTES = 64 KiB, summed over every island the creator ever published, withdrawn and removed ones included, because nothing is deleted. A withdrawn island frees its slot, but its bytes still count (workshop.mjs:36, 133-139). Cleared: the creator's re-simulated replay gets any grade but foiled and banks loot (workshop.mjs:64-66). Report reasons: unfair, unplayable, copied, offensive, other (workshop.mjs:58). Spike: at least 50 completions in a day and more than 5 times the island's daily mean over the week before; the island is flagged and queued for a person (workshop.mjs:50-51, spike()). Remix: the new island names its original (remix_of) and earns the original nothing.

options.means: The document states the server's figures: word lists as in server/src/words.json (16 adjectives × 16 nouns, both launch languages); 5 published islands, 8 for a Builder; a 64 KiB lifetime quota per account that counts everything ever published; 'cleared' means the creator's own run banks loot at any grade but foiled; five report reasons (unfair, unplayable, copied, offensive, other); a spike is a day with 50 or more completions and more than 5 times the previous week's daily mean; a remix names its original and pays it nothing.
options.consequences: Nothing changes in the build. The name pool is small and shared with constellations. Two islands are more likely than not to share a name by about the 19th island, and at 10,000 published islands each name is used about 39 times. The quota is a lifetime cap: at the example island's size a creator can publish about 133 times in total. One who withdraws and republishes to fix an island three times a week reaches that within a year and can never publish again. At §24.1's 10 KB per island only 6 fit, fewer than a Builder's 8 slots.

G27.question: How are the six leagues' Renown boundaries set: fitted to §14.7's season-end shares as built, fitted to §14.7's arrival times, recomputed each season from rank, or refitted after a change to the Renown rules?
G27.why_it_matters: The server cannot place anyone in a league without boundaries, and the document gives none. §14.7 gives two targets: when an engaged player arrives in each league, and each league's share at season end. F40 shows both cannot hold at once under the current Renown rules. The item also leaves open what Dust, Ember and Tide earn at season end, where about two players in three finish, and whether Renown is kept in whole points.
G27.today: server/src/leagues.json, generated by tools/league_model.py and checked by tools/check_all.sh, starts the leagues at Dust 0, Ember 128, Tide 184, Star 300, Nova 644 and Paradox 1,160, with each league's divisions at thirds of its span. server/src/seasons.mjs rounds each Renown amount to the nearest whole point (lines 29-30, 144). Star, Nova and Paradox earn a cosmetic of their league and the season, and the other three earn nothing (reward(), seasons.mjs:46-53). At season end Renown is pulled halfway back toward the lower boundary of the league the player ended in (pulledBack(), lines 101-107). Seasons run back to back from RULEBORN_SEASON_START (server/README.md).

Renown is kept in whole points. Only Star, Nova and Paradox earn season-end cosmetics. The pull-back floor is the lower boundary of the league the player ended in.
options.consequences: Season-end shares match §14.7. An engaged player arrives much sooner than §14.7 says: Ember on day 2, Tide on day 4, Star on day 8 and Nova on day 57, against the first week, week 3, month 2 and month 3 (F40). The climb is fast for the first week and then stalls for about seven weeks. The lower three leagues, about 64% of players at season end, earn nothing.

Fitted season-end shares (league_model.py output): Dust 3.5%, Ember 29.7%, Tide 30.8%, Star 25.7%, Nova 9.0%, Paradox 1.3%; Dust, Ember and Tide together 64.0%. Under the model's three alternative assumptions the boundaries move by up to 25% (Star 300 → 375 with more engaged players), the others by 13% or less. §14.7's shares sum to 96%, so Dust's target is the other 4%.

options.label: Fit to the arrival times
options.means: Boundaries are set so an engaged player arrives when §14.7's first column says: Ember in the first week, Tide by week 3, Star around month 2, Nova from month 3. The shares column becomes an outcome, not a target.

options.means: There are no fixed Renown boundaries. At a fixed interval (for example daily) and at season end, the server places players by rank among the season's active players: top 1% Paradox, next 10% Nova, 25% Star, 30% Tide and 30% Ember. Dust and Ember floors still stop a player falling below them.

Separately, §18.1's 'rewards are given by league' reads as every league earning something, so give Dust to Tide a small season cosmetic, since about two players in three end there.

Design targets for the Renown formula in 12.9.
Star, Nova and Paradox leagues with season-end cosmetics.

F37.question: Where does a player who never raids get the experience and pages that let them progress?
F37.why_it_matters: §14.4 promises that a non-raider restores the launch 24 laws in about 80 days and the full Codex in about 195, from the Library alone. Under the document's own gates, that player earns almost nothing. The Library opens at Keeper 4. Experience from spending is capped by the Spire, which Keeper levels gate. Experience from restoring laws needs pages. In the model the non-raider stalls at Keeper 2. That makes two claims false today: §10.4's claim that the Library is 'the whole of a non-raider's progression' (the floor §14.4 says 13.3 rests on), and §7.6's promise that raiding is 'not the only' path. Even without the gates, §10.4's school rule caps the Library at 12 of the launch 24. The model also leaves out §14.4's 3 pages for a Lab experiment that finds nothing. A non-raider can reach that source without a heist, and pages are how a non-raider earns experience.
F37.today: The server grants no Keeper experience; progression exists only in the economy model. tools/economy_model/data.py:286 defines the never_raids archetype (5 sessions, 0 heists, 3 Lab experiments). model.py pages_today() (lines 579-595) gives it the Library alone. Its docstring says Lab experiments that find nothing and first meetings with a law are left out. Run for 400 days, the archetype ends at Keeper 2 (reached on day 3) with the 3 starting laws, because it never reaches the Library's Keeper 4 gate. test_economy_model.py (around line 411) asserts it stays below Keeper 12 and never restores the Codex. docs/design/generated/pacing.md prints 'never (F37)' for both Codex rows.

options.label: Keep the build's reading: Library alone
options.means: A non-raider earns only the Library's pages, as §14.4 says. The Library is gated at Keeper 4 and there is no other experience source, so they stall at Keeper 2 with the three starting laws.
options.consequences: There is no way to progress without raiding. §14.4's 80 and 195 days, §10.4's 'the whole of a non-raider's progression' and §7.6's 'not the only one' all become false and must be withdrawn. Players who prefer building stall on day 3. The soft-launch trigger that compares non-raider retention with raider retention has nothing to measure.
options.numbers: Model run, never_raids, 400 days: Keeper 2 (reached day 3), 3 laws, no milestones.
options.doc_edit: §14.4: replace both never-raids lines with 'a player who never raids does not progress past Keeper 2'. §10.4 and §7.6 drop the non-raider claim.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does

options.label: Library plus daily goals; launch 24 is the ceiling
options.means: The non-raider's floor is the page sources §14.4's table already lists that need no heist: the Library, plus daily goals worth about 2 pages a day. At least one goal each day needs no heist. Goal pages go to the law the player has marked as the one they are working on, whatever its school. This is the same idea as §7.6's bad-luck floor, and it is how a non-raider gets laws outside their three starting schools. Recommended addition: the tutorial's two Drifting ruins (§16: the first heist at 2:00 and a second ruin at 7:00, both on day 1) pay §14.2's successful-heist experience. Later ruins keep §12.10's pages and Essence and pay no experience; paying it on every ruin is option C. Ruins are counted apart from §14.1's heists a day, which are raids on player islands, echoes and 12.22's fallback targets. A ruin charges no entry fee and never uses up one of G20 C's 20 paid raids, even when it fills a thin target list (12.22). Its Essence counts only toward G20 C's currency backstop (33.3 × B a week). Later chapters (Keeper 12 and up) need heists.
options.consequences: Plain B: a non-raider reaches Keeper 8 on day 46 and restores all 24 launch laws by about day 78, against §14.4's 80. Then they plateau for good, with the Keeper bar at 937 of the 1,020 XP to Keeper 9 and the Spire stuck at level 2. §14.8's home screen, which shows the nearest goal, would then show '83 XP to go' forever. With the tutorial-ruin addition, the same player reaches Keeper 11 on day 87 with Spire 3 open, and plateaus on a fresh bar (1 XP toward Keeper 12). If the tutorial ruins paid only the foiled-heist rate, the bar would stop 19 XP short of Keeper 9, which is worse. Without the working-on routing, the Library-style school rule stops the player at 12 launch laws, and pages that land in unwanted schools make the 78 days late. The non-raider never opens chapter 3, so every season's new laws need heists. Because ruins sit outside §14.1's counts, the two tutorial ruins are extra experience for every player, not only the non-raider. That moves the generated tables by about a day: Keeper 40 for the engaged player goes from day 357 to 358 at the low edge and from 349 to 348 at the top, and the regular player's from 440 to 439 at the top (446 at the low edge does not move). A few purchase rows move more, because buying order shifts (the casual player's Vault level 2 goes from day 27 to 39 at the low edge). G20 C's 20-raid week is untouched, because no ruin counts toward it. Empty Lab experiments (§14.4's 3 pages) would only make the plateau come sooner.

At +2 a day: Keeper 3 on day 6, 4 on day 8, 8 on day 46, then no further (keeper_xp 937 of KEEPER_XP_TO_NEXT[7] = 1,020); 12 laws on day 25, 24 laws on day 78. Every archetype with two extra successful heists' experience on day 1, full Codex, both edges (engaged 420 days, regular 520, casual 400): Keeper 40 engaged 357 to 358 (low) and 349 to 348 (top); regular 446 unchanged (low) and 440 to 439 (top); engaged full Codex 92 unchanged (low) and 92 to 90 (top); casual full Codex 241 to 239 (low) and 240 to 239 (top). options.label: Ruins pay heist experience every day

Every table that moves is republished.

options.consequences: Building a strong defence becomes a path of its own, which fits §13's 'defence is designed'. But progress depends on how often other players raid you, which the player does not control, and a weak island earns almost nothing. It cannot be priced without a raid rate. It also opens a way to farm experience: friends can fail raids against each other on purpose.

recommendation.rationale: B, with the tutorial's two ruins paying successful-heist experience and daily-goal pages going to the law the player is working on. This makes §14.4's launch promise true (the launch 24 in about 76–78 days against the stated 80) using systems §14.6 and §7.6 already have. Ruins are counted apart from §14.1's raids, so they never use up one of G20 C's 20 paid raids; the cost is that the tutorial ruins move the published tables by about a day. It adds one testable assertion, which suits one-developer scope. The player-experience and scope judges both chose B. The player-experience judge added the tutorial-ruin experience so the non-raider plateaus on a fresh bar at Keeper 11 with Spire 3 open, not frozen at 937 of 1,020 XP. That judge also had §14.1's counts include ruins; the brief does not, because G20 C's 20-raid week is built on §14.1's four raids. The scope judge added the page routing and the test. The balance judge dissented for C at the foiled-heist rate, correctly showing that no page source moves B's plateau past Keeper 8. That leaves chapter 3, season laws and §14.4's 195-day Codex out of a non-raider's reach, and §32's Library-output trigger cannot fix it. It stays the upgrade path if the owner wants non-raiders to reach the full Codex (day 175, raiding still about twice as fast). Confidence is medium because the dissent concerns what the floor is for, not a factual error.

quotes.text: A player who never raids earns the Library alone, which is the floor the whole design rests on (13.3)
Never raids: the Library alone, averaging about 6 a day while it is levelled out of production income — about 195 days
| A Lab experiment that finds nothing
Keeper experience comes from successful heists (30 + 6 × Keeper level), foiled heists (10 + 2 × level), spending (1 for every 40 Starlight) and restoring laws (60 + 10 × level).
It is the only page source that does not require raiding, which makes it the whole of a non-raider's progression
Pages from the Library are drawn from schools the player already has laws in, so it deepens what someone is building rather than handing them new directions.
Drifting ruins: three universes built by the game each day, for pages and Essence but no Renown.
Raiding is the efficient path, not the only one.
Every eighth heist guarantees a page of a law you are actually working on
| Two more ruins appear. The player chooses one and runs it alone.
Day 2: the first heist against another player's universe.
Only then do the filters widen, in order — rating, then Keeper level, then Renown — and ruins fill what remains (12.10).

F37.also_needed: Whatever the option: whether an empty Lab pairing can be re-run for §14.4's 3 pages, and at what rate experiments find nothing (the model leaves these out). For B: confirmation that daily goals always include one that needs no heist and that its pages go to the law the player is working on, and whether the tutorial's two ruins pay §14.2's successful-heist experience, which only works at the successful rate. panel.variant: B, with one addition that removes a stuck progress bar. §14.2 states that a ruin heist pays heist experience like any other heist, so the tutorial's ruins count, and §14.1 states that its heists-a-day counts include ruins. The economy model gives the never_raids archetype the experience from the tutorial's ruins; the engaged tables already book experience for every heist from day 1, so they are unchanged. My rerun, with 2 goal pages a day, 1 successful ruin on each of days 1 and 2, and the rest of the model unchanged: Keeper 8 on day 39, 9 on day 77, 10 on day 82, 11 on day 87, then a plateau with a fresh bar (1 XP toward 12). Spire 3 opens, and the launch 24 are restored on day 76. Plain B plateaus at Keeper 8 on day 46 with 937 of the 1,020 XP to Keeper 9 and never gains more. Everything else in B stays the same: at least one daily goal a day needs no heist, and goal pages may be of any school. §14.4 says later chapters need heists, and the 195-day line goes.
panel.reasoning: Through the player lens, the useful question is what a builder who never raids sees on the home screen, week after week. Option A shows it stuck on day 3. That breaks §7.6's own rule, "Raiding is the efficient path, not the only one.", and the reason §7.6 gives for it: "gating a resource behind one activity is where players stop feeling directed and start feeling forced [210]". C serves a player who avoids other players' islands, but it leaves the player who never heists at Keeper 2, so §14.4 and §10.4 still need rewriting. D ties a builder's progress to how often strangers attack them, which the builder cannot control, and nobody can price it. B is the only option that makes the launch promise true using systems the document already has (§14.6 daily goals already include non-heist goals such as "birth a ruleborn"). I reran the model: at +2 pages a day, the launch 24 are done by day 78 against §14.4's 80, and Keeper 8 comes on day 46. The pages must be allowed from any school, or §10.4's school rule stops the player at 12 laws. Plain B has a flaw I found in the rerun (the scratch script is at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Ruleborn/4036626a-ccc0-53cd-b585-d7b6007ab17e/scratchpad/brief/f37_px.py). The player stops at 937 of 1,020 XP toward Keeper 9, which is the level that opens Spire 3 (data.SPIRE_KEEPER_LEVEL = 1, 5, 9, 13), and stays there. At +11 pages a day they stop at 857 of 1,020. §14.8's rule "| The home screen surfaces whichever goal is closest to done, whatever kind it is." would then show "83 XP to go" forever, a goal that can never be reached. That is the opposite of what §14.8 wants. If the tutorial's ruins pay experience, which is the plain reading of §14.2's "successful heists" and matches §12.10's "They carry the tutorial and give new players safe practice with unfamiliar laws.", the same player reaches Keeper 11 and Spire 3, and the stop falls on a fresh bar instead. The engaged pacing tables don't move, and nothing new has to be built, which fits one-developer scope. Confidence: medium.

panel.variant: Drifting ruins pay experience at §14.2's existing foiled-heist rate (10 + 2 × Keeper level) rather than the successful-heist rate (30 + 6 × level). Their pages, which §12.10 already grants, are booked as well. For the published tables, §14.1's heist counts are raids, and the never_raids archetype is priced as 3 ruins a day plus daily goals (about 2 pages), with no haul and no Renown. Ruin pages come from laws the player has not met (§12.12: the game "draws from what they haven't"), so they also get around §10.4's owned-school rule without a separate exception. Economy model, never_raids, low edge, 700 days, with pages_today and award_xp patched for the archetype (scratch scripts in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Ruleborn/4036626a-ccc0-53cd-b585-d7b6007ab17e/scratchpad/brief/f37_low.py): 3 ruins a day at the foiled rate gives Keeper 8 on day 12, Keeper 12 on day 34, the launch 24 on day 34, Keeper 24 and the full 48-law Codex on day 175 (§14.4 states about 195), and Keeper 40 on day 511. The engaged raider in the same model gets the full Codex on day 92 and Keeper 40 on day 357. At 1 ruin a day it gives the launch 24 on day 54 and the full Codex on day 512. The doc edits are §12.10, "ruins pay §14.2's foiled-heist experience", and §14.4's never-raids lines restated as "daily goals and Drifting ruins, besides the Library: the launch 24 in about 34 days, the full Codex in about 175".
panel.reasoning:
B's plateau is structural, and no page source can fix it. In the model the non-raider's experience comes only from restoring laws, which stops once the 24 laws of the first two chapters are restored, and from spending, which the Spire caps (it is stuck at level 2). I reran the model at +1, +2, +5 and +11 pages a day, and it stopped at Keeper 8 every time. It never opens chapter 3, never gets a season's new laws, and never reaches §14.4's 195-day Codex. The soft-launch trigger in §32 ("the Library’s page output moves up one level-step each season") cannot move a Keeper plateau, so under B the only fix the document plans for non-raider retention would do nothing.

Only an experience source tied to a heist gets past Keeper 8. Ruins already exist (§12.10, three a day, pages and Essence), carry the tutorial, and involve no victim. That makes them the non-PvP play §7.6 means when it says raiding is "not the only" path for "the many players who prefer building", and it adds no system, which suits one-developer scope.

The brief's C at the full successful-heist rate is too generous. With 3 ruins a day the non-raider fills the full Codex on day 88, ahead of the engaged raider's day 92, which breaks §7.6's "Raiding is the efficient path". Paying §14.2's foiled rate uses a figure the document already has. It lands the full Codex on day 175 against the stated 195, and raiding stays about twice as fast (day 92 against 175).

D cannot be priced: the document states no rate at which an island is raided, and the player does not control it. A (keep the build) breaks §7.6, §10.4 and §14.4 outright.

panel.variant: B, tightened so it can be tested. (1) The pages from the non-heist daily goal go to the law the player marks as the one they are working on, the same idea §7.6 already uses for its bad-luck floor ("Every eighth heist guarantees a page of a law you are actually working on", line 2199). The model pools pages across schools, and this rule makes that pooling true, so the model's 78 days become exact and not just the fastest case. It also settles "any school" with one rule, where a picker by school would need its own design. (2) The model's non-raider floor counts only daily goals (+2 a day). Empty Lab experiments stay out of the floor, because the document states no rate at which an experiment finds nothing. They are extra on top, so the published days still err low. (3) Replace the test_economy_model.py assertion "stalls below Keeper 12" (lines ~409-412) with two: never_raids restores the launch 24 by about day 80, and plateaus at Keeper 8 on the full Codex. The document's sentence then has a test that fails if later tuning breaks it.
panel.reasoning:
Seen through scope and build risk, B is the only option that keeps §14.4's promise without a new system and without moving the engaged player's published tables. I re-ran the model (rerun.run('never_raids','low',600) with +2 pages a day for the archetype only). It gives Keeper 3 on day 6, Keeper 4 on day 8, Keeper 8 on day 46 and no higher. It reaches 12 laws on day 25 and the launch 24 on day 78, against the document's 80. At +1 a day it reaches the launch 24 on day 97. At +11 a day it reaches Keeper 8 on day 19 and the launch 24 on day 33. The plateau is Keeper 8 every time, because Spire 3 needs Keeper 10 (design line 5596) and spending experience is capped by the Spire.

The daily-goal system is already in scope: §14.6 lists goals like "birth a ruleborn" that need no heist. So B adds one content rule (always offer one non-heist goal) and one page-routing rule, not a new engine path. The model change is one line in pages_today() (tools/economy_model/model.py:579-595), and the plateau can be asserted in a test.

C looks cheap but is not. The build must decide whether §14.1's heist counts include ruins, and if they don't, every pacing table in §14.2, §14.3 and §10.2 moves and must be regenerated and republished. G22 already says those tables move by months on unstated assumptions, and C adds another. It also does nothing for someone who never heists at all.

D cannot be tested. It rests on a raid rate the document never states and the model cannot derive. It adds a server path to credit experience to the defender in Service.grant. It also opens a collusion exploit (friends failing raids on purpose to farm experience) that one developer would have to police.

A costs no build work but removes the floor that §13.3 and §10.4 rest on. It also makes the soft-launch trigger that compares non-raider and raider retention (design line 15362) meaningless, so it saves code by breaking a pillar.

The honest cost of B is that the document must say plainly that a non-raider plateaus at Keeper 8 and that chapter 3 and every season's new laws need raiding. The 195-day line has to go.

G22.question: Which staffing order, realm-opening order and Guardian Post staffing should §14.1 state as the basis for the published pacing tables?
G22.why_it_matters: §14.2 says the Keeper and milestone tables are the economy model's output, but three choices that move them by months are not stated in §14.1: which producer a new worker staffs, which realm types open first, and whether posts are staffed. Across these choices Keeper 40 moves from day 337 to day 1,113. Until they are written down, the tables describe a player the document never defines.
G22.today: tools/economy_model/config.py sets staffing_order = 'heart_first' (the Heart first, then each realm, Well, Spring, Garden; line 119). realm_order is (aether, starlight, essence, aether, starlight, essence), the median of all 90 orders (line 110). staff_posts = False (line 122). options.label: Keep the build's reading

options.consequences: The tables stay as generated: Keeper 40 on day 357, everything built on day 719, the 38th character on day 249. They describe a player who leaves every Guardian Post empty. A player who staffs every post reaches Keeper 40 on day 1,113 and never builds everything, so a player who guards trades pace for defence.
options.numbers: pacing.md, engaged player, band's lower edge: 357 / 719 / 249; with every post staffed, 1113 / never / never.
options.doc_edit: §14.1 'Logic: what the model assumes': three sentences (staffing Heart first, median realm order, posts unstaffed). Pacing sentences quoting Keeper 40 move to day 357 under §14.2's rule.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does

options.label: Build's staffing, realm order as a band
options.means: As A for staffing and posts, but realm order is left to the player and published as a band across all 90 orders.
options.consequences: The tables show the player's choice honestly: Keeper 40 between day 337 and 385, everything built between day 667 and 788. Opening both Starlight realms first is fastest. Each milestone becomes a range across two dimensions (§9.6's attempt band and realm order), which is harder to read.
options.numbers: pacing.md: Keeper 40 on day 337–385 and everything built on day 667–788 across 90 orders (rerun.py realm_order_spread).
options.doc_edit: §14.1: staffing and posts sentences as in A, plus 'realm order is the player's; tables give its spread'. §14.2 and §14.3 tables gain the realm-order range.
options.build_change: rerun.py prints the realm-order spread for every milestone, not only for Keeper 40 and everything built, and the table check compares both edges.

options.label: Even staffing
options.means: A new worker goes to each producer in turn (one each), not Heart first. Posts are unstaffed, and the realm order is the median.
options.consequences: This is what a player who spreads workers does. Pacing is slower: Keeper 40 on day 424 (+67 days), everything built on day 877 (+158), the 38th character on day 276 (+27).
options.doc_edit: §14.1: 'workers are spread one to each producer in turn'. Every pacing table is regenerated, and sentences that quote them move.
options.build_change: config.py staffing_order = 'even'. Re-run the model and republish pacing.md and the document tables.

options.label: Staff every post
options.means: One ruleborn stands at every Guardian Post built, taken from production, as §13.4's 'hold stability only while staffed' suggests a defending player does.
options.consequences: The economy does not finish: Keeper 40 on day 1,113, and never everything built or the 38th character. This is §5.8's settled scarcity at work (F1): 38 ruleborn cannot staff every producer and every post. Choosing this means the post rule or the roster size must change before any pacing table can be published.
options.numbers: pacing.md: 1113 / never / never.
options.doc_edit: §14.1: 'posts are staffed'. Then §13.4 or §9.5 changes (for example, posts draw on guards who do not work), and the whole re-run is republished.

recommendation.rationale: Heart-first staffing and the median realm order are reasonable readings where §9.2 and §5.2 leave the choice to the player, and writing them down turns the published tables into a stated design position with no re-run. Keep §14.2's single band so the tables stay readable, and add one sentence giving the realm-order spread (Keeper 40 on day 337–385). under-staffing is normal, and choosing which producer goes short is the decision

wards and posts are built with Starlight (10.2) and hold stability only while staffed

When the regenerated curve breaks a pacing sentence anywhere in this document, the sentence moves, never the table.

C42.question: What is the chance that a heist finds a stray, and does a bonus-page chance sit beside it or share it?
C42.why_it_matters: §11.5 says one heist in eight finds a stray. §14.6 says one in eight finds a stray or a bonus page, which makes strays rarer, perhaps one in sixteen. The odds are shown to players in the Codex, so the game must display one number, and the economy model needs one rate.
C42.today: The server and simulation grant no heist strays; the only stray the server grants is at the top of the season track (server/src/track.mjs:51). The economy model takes §11.5 and reads it as one in eight successful heists: HEIST_STRAY_CHANCE = 1/8 (tools/economy_model/data.py:503), with no bonus-page roll. In the model, a stray found with no free home waits until one frees up (model.py _strays()). pacing.md shows that halving the rate to one in sixteen moves nothing it publishes (357 / 719 / 249 either way), because homes, not strays, limit the roster (F38).

options.label: Keep the build's reading: §11.5's rate
options.means: One successful heist in eight finds a stray. There is no separate bonus-page surprise; the Lucky trait's 10% bonus page (§11.3) stays the only one.
options.consequences: An engaged player finds about 0.3 to 0.4 strays a day (4 heists × 60–80% success × 1/8). The Codex shows 'one in eight'. The published pacing does not move. Once the roster is full (around day 249, F38), a stray has no home and the document does not say what it becomes, so §14.6's only surprise needs a rule for that case.
options.numbers: 4 × 0.8 × 1/8 = 0.40 and 4 × 0.6 × 1/8 = 0.30 strays a day (§14.1 heists, §14.5 success arc). pacing.md: 357 / 719 / 249; 38th character on day 249.
options.doc_edit: §14.6: 'any successful heist has about a one-in-eight chance of a stray, with the odds shown in the Codex' (drop 'or a bonus page'). §11.5: add 'successful'.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does

options.label: §14.6's shared one in eight
options.means: One heist in eight gives a surprise, split evenly: one in sixteen a stray, one in sixteen a bonus page.
options.consequences: Strays arrive half as often (about 0.15 to 0.2 a day for an engaged player), and a bonus page adds about 0.15 to 0.2 pages a day, around 1% of the ~16 a day §14.4 gives. Nothing published moves. Late in the game the bonus page keeps a surprise possible once the roster is full.
options.numbers: 4 × (0.6–0.8) × 1/16 ≈ 0.15–0.20 of each a day. pacing.md's 'one in sixteen' row: 357 / 719 / 249.
options.doc_edit: §11.5: 'About one successful heist in sixteen finds a stray'. §14.6 stays, with the split stated.
options.build_change: data.py HEIST_STRAY_CHANCE = 1/16, plus a bonus-page term of 1/16 a success in pages_today(). The server's grant rolls one surprise when heist strays are built.

options.label: Two separate one-in-eight chances
options.means: Every successful heist rolls twice: one in eight for a stray and, independently, one in eight for a bonus page.
options.consequences: Strays arrive as in A, plus about 0.3 to 0.4 extra pages a day for an engaged player, around 2% of the page economy. The Codex shows two odds. The extra pages move the Codex days slightly earlier, so the Codex rows need a re-run.
options.doc_edit: §14.6: 'one in eight a stray and, separately, one in eight a bonus page'. §14.4's page table gains a row.
options.build_change: data.py: a PAGES_BONUS term in pages_today(), then re-run the Codex rows. The server's grant rolls both when built.

recommendation.rationale: It keeps the rate §11.5 already owns and the model already uses, gives the Codex one honest number (fairness), and moves nothing published. A bonus page is already the Lucky trait's job, so a second page roll adds a rule without a purpose. The full-roster case is F38's to settle, for example by having strays wait for a free home, as the model does.

quotes.text: Strays found on heists. About one heist in eight finds a stray in the target universe; carrying it out adds it to the roster with three traits, one of them rare.
No reward for logging in. Surprises replace it: any heist has about a one-in-eight chance of a stray or a bonus page, with the odds shown in the Codex.
Lucky: 10% chance of a bonus page.

G21.question: What is one target list's 'difficulty band', and how often are the lists rebuilt?
G21.why_it_matters: §24.8 makes target selection a cached file 'per difficulty band', 'generated periodically', and defines neither. The band decides how big each file is and what the device must filter itself. The rebuild period decides how long a republished island's old snapshot stays offered, and how many database rows every rebuild reads. In this build that read count grows through each season (see G33).
G21.today: server/src/service.mjs targetLists() (line 214) builds one list per realm level ('realm-level-N', or the snapshot's own band column when set). Each entry carries the island's Glicko rating and deviation, Keeper level and Renown, so the device applies §12.22's filters itself. A new player's islands are left off the lists while their shield holds (matchmaking.mjs shielded(): their first 72 hours or until their first raid). Lists are content-addressed, so an unchanged band keeps its edge cache. A band keeps its current and previous list, and a band with no islands left loses its list. server/src/main.mjs:181-184 rebuilds every 15 minutes (TARGET_LISTS_MS) and once at start. A lease on a snapshot no island holds any more is granted as an echo (§12.3) for 14 days after it was published: the raider is paid a haul, but no Renown moves, and the owner is not paid, rated or notified. After 14 days, and always for a trace or a friendly heist, it is refused as 'superseded' (service.mjs:346-365, 626-653). For each listed island a rebuild calls seasons.league(owner), which re-sums every Renown row the owner has this season (renownIn(), seasons.mjs:109-115).

options.label: Keep the build's reading
options.means: A band is a realm level, the unit of §12.22's success-band guarantee. Each list carries every entry's rating for the device to filter. Lists are rebuilt every 15 minutes, and each entry's Renown is re-summed from the owner's Renown rows at every rebuild.
options.consequences: A republished island's old snapshot stays offered for at most 15 minutes. A raider who leases it in that window plays an echo: they are paid a haul, no Renown moves, and nothing is taken from the owner. Reads grow through the season. At mid-season a rebuild reads about 63 to 231 rows per island, about 6,000 to 22,000 a day, so the free plan's 5 million reads a day run out at about 230 to 830 islands, before any heist. At 1,000,000 islands on the paid plan, rebuilds alone cost about $156 to $640 a month in reads.
options.numbers: 96 rebuilds a day (main.mjs:181-184). Fixed rows per island per rebuild: the islands, snapshots and accounts join (3), shielded() (1), islandRating() (1), the current season (1) and the standing (1) = 7. Renown rows: renownIn() reads every row the owner has this season, so at R rows a day there are 28 × R at mid-season. R = 2 to 8 is an assumption: each raid books one row for the raider and usually one for the defender, at §14.1's 1 heist a day (casual) to 4 (engaged). (7 + 56) × 96 = 6,048 and (7 + 224) × 96 = 22,176 a day; 5,000,000 ÷ 6,048 ≈ 830 and ÷ 22,176 ≈ 225 islands (§28.3 free plan). Paid: 10^6 × 6,048 × 30 = 1.8 × 10^11 and 10^6 × 22,176 × 30 = 6.7 × 10^11 a month, less 2.5 × 10^10 included, at $0.001 per million ≈ $156 and $640 (§28.3). Writes: one target_lists row per band per rebuild (load.json 'target lists (x96)': 96 a day), plus one standings row for each listed owner not yet seen in the current season, written by the first rebuild after a rollover (seasons.mjs standing(), reached from service.mjs:236).
options.doc_edit: §24.8: 'A band is a realm level; each list carries its islands' ratings so the device filters; lists are rebuilt every fifteen minutes.' §24.8's snapshots row: 'difficulty band' becomes 'realm level'.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does

options.label: Realm level, rebuilt hourly
options.means: A band is a realm level, as built, but lists are rebuilt once an hour.
options.consequences: A republished island's old version stays listed for up to an hour. A raider who picks it plays an echo: they are paid a haul, no Renown moves, and nothing is taken from the owner. A new player's island is shielded for their first 72 hours or until their first raid, so a slower rebuild rarely delays it. An established player's newly opened realm can wait up to an hour to become a target. The Renown on each entry, which the device filters to within 150, can be up to an hour old. Rows read by rebuilds fall to a quarter: at mid-season the free plan's reads last to about 900 to 3,300 islands as built, or about 29,800 if each player's Renown is kept as a running total.
options.numbers: 24 rebuilds a day: (7 + 56) × 24 = 1,512 and (7 + 224) × 24 = 5,544 rows per island per day; 5,000,000 ÷ 1,512 ≈ 3,300 and ÷ 5,544 ≈ 900. With a running Renown total, 7 × 24 = 168 a day; 5,000,000 ÷ 168 ≈ 29,800 (at 15 minutes, 7 × 96 = 672 a day and ≈ 7,440). NEW_PLAYER_SHIELD_HOURS = 72 (server/src/facts.json).
options.doc_edit: §24.8 as in A, with 'every hour'.
options.build_change: main.mjs: TARGET_LISTS_MS = 60 × 60 × 1000 for the lists. The season rollover keeps its own 15-minute interval, since today it shares the same constant.

options.label: Realm level × rating band
options.means: A band is a realm level cut again by Glicko-2 rating (§12.22 step 1's 'within one band'), so the device downloads only targets of nearby difficulty. Lists are rebuilt every 15 minutes.
options.consequences: Downloads are smaller. Files multiply (realm levels × rating bands), and a thin cell is more often empty, so the device more often fetches other files for §12.22 step 4's fallbacks and widening. Rows read per rebuild are unchanged, and rows written grow by one per cell per rebuild.
options.numbers: No band width is stated anywhere; the count of files is realm levels × rating bands.
options.doc_edit: §24.8: 'A band is a realm level and a rating band of N points'. §12.22 step 1 names the same width.
options.build_change: service.targetLists() keys lists by realm level and rating bucket. The device fetches the neighbouring buckets when widening.

recommendation.rationale: Realm level is the unit of §12.22's guarantee, and the build already carries ratings so the device can filter, so the band should stay as built. Hourly rebuilds cut the rows that rebuilds read fourfold, and players see little of the cost: a new player is shielded anyway, and a stale entry is played as an echo that pays a haul and takes nothing from its owner. That fits §24.1's goal that the free tier carries the early game. Separately, and needing no decision, the build should keep each player's season Renown as a running total on the standing row. That is the larger saving: about 7 reads per island per rebuild instead of up to about 230 at mid-season.

quotes.text: Target selection is a file, not a query. Candidate lists per difficulty band are generated periodically as static objects, so choosing a target costs a cached download rather than a database search.
the middle of the list is drawn from the raider-success band for the target's realm level — 60 to 75% at realm level 1, 55 to 70% from realm level 2 (13.2)
Bundle hash as the key, realm type, difficulty band, when published. Never edited
Robbing an echo takes nothing from its owner; its loot is created by the game.

G21.also_needed: For C, a rating band width in Glicko-2 points.

G33.question: Should §24.1 budget rows read as well as rows written, and must the load test be re-run on the edge platform before its figures are trusted?
G33.why_it_matters: §24.1 budgets only writes. But the database plan §28.3 cites bills rows read too, and caps the free plan at 5 million a day, and nothing measures them. The load test runs on local Node and SQLite, so its figures are a lower bound: index writes are not counted, fees and hauls are not booked, and its CPU time is not an edge isolate's. §24.1's cost table could be wrong at scale without anyone seeing it. The target-list rebuild (G21) is already a read cost that grows with the number of islands and through the season.
G33.today: server/load.mjs plays §14.1's players through the service for 3 days (60 players per archetype) and counts SQLite's changes as rows written. It says so at line 16: 'Rows read are not measured'. It prices monthly players with §25.1's one-in-three daily share (facts DAILY_SHARE, load.mjs:140). server/load.json: engaged players write 46.01 rows a day against a budget of 5 (9.2×), regular 23.58, casual 10.53. Re-simulation takes p50 15 ms (p95 20.9 ms) against the free plan's 10 ms, so validationFitsFreePlan is false. The paid plan at 1,000,000 monthly players costs $415 a month if all are engaged, $191 if regular, $60 if casual. Its raiders hold no Starlight, so no fee is booked, and its drawn raids are foiled, so no haul is booked.

options.label: Keep the build's reading
options.means: §24.1 budgets writes only. The load test stays local: SQLite's change count as rows written, local Node CPU, no rows read, raiders without Starlight. Its figures are read as a lower bound.
options.consequences: No new work. Reads stay unbudgeted. Per row, a read costs a thousandth of a write on the paid plan, but one read pattern grows with islands × rebuilds rather than with play. The target-list rebuild reads about 6,000 to 22,000 rows per island per day at mid-season (G21). That exhausts the free plan's daily cap at a few hundred islands and costs about $156 to $640 a month at 1,000,000 islands. Writes and CPU are understated by an unknown factor.
options.numbers: server/load.json as above. Reads $0.001 and writes $1.00 per million past the paid allowance (§28.3). Rebuild reads from G21.
options.doc_edit: §24.1: one sentence saying the budget covers writes and that the load test's figures are a local lower bound.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does

options.label: Budget reads, measure locally
options.means: §24.1 adds a rows-read budget per active player per day, and the load test counts reads locally by wrapping every query and counting the rows it visits. It also gives raiders Starlight and lets some drawn raids succeed, so fees and hauls are booked, and it measures a late-season state as well as the first days.
options.consequences: Reads become a checked design constraint, and check_all fails a change that adds reads, as it already does for writes. The run must include a population with weeks of Renown rows (for example 56 days); otherwise a 3-day run cannot see the rebuild cost that grows through a season. Figures remain SQLite's, not D1's billing, and CPU remains this machine's.
options.numbers: Candidate budgets from the plans: the free plan's 5,000,000 reads a day ÷ 3,333 daily players (10,000 monthly ÷ 3) = 1,500 per player-day. The paid plan's 25 billion a month ÷ (333,333 daily × 30) = 2,500 per player-day at 1,000,000 monthly. §24.1 and §28.3 give the plan figures; §25.1 gives the one-in-three share.
options.doc_edit: §24.1 Budget line: 'and N row reads per active player per day', with the plan arithmetic. The load test is named as what checks it.
options.build_change: load.mjs: a counting wrapper on db.prepare, reads recorded in load.json and checked, and a late-season scenario. Raiders are seeded with Starlight and a share of drawn raids succeed.

options.label: Budget reads, run on the edge
options.means: As B, plus the load test is run on the edge platform itself (Workers with D1) before soft launch. D1 reports the rows read and written it bills, index writes included, and the CPU a real isolate uses. Those figures replace the local ones in §24.1.
options.consequences: The cost table rests on billed numbers, and the 15 ms against 10 ms CPU question (F47) gets a real answer. The paid Workers plan ($5 a month) is needed at launch anyway, because re-simulation already exceeds the free plan's CPU. The added cost is the work of deploying the server as an edge function and writing a load driver that runs against it. The run also shows whether the target-list rebuild, which issues several queries per island, fits in a scheduled edge invocation at all.
options.numbers: Plan figures as in B. Paid plan $5 a month, $0.001 per million reads and $1.00 per million writes past the allowance (§28.3). load.json: p50 15 ms, p95 20.9 ms against 10 ms.
options.doc_edit: §24.1 as in B, plus 'measured on the edge platform before soft launch'. The monthly cost table is recomputed from the edge run.
options.build_change: As B, plus a Workers and D1 deployment of server/src/http.mjs and a load driver that runs against it, with its figures recorded in server/load.json.

options.label: Run on the edge, writes and CPU only
options.means: As C, but §24.1 still budgets writes only. The edge run reports rows read, with no budget and no check.
options.consequences: Billed writes (index writes included) and isolate CPU become known. Reads are visible in each run but unchecked, so a change like G21's per-rebuild Renown sum can add reads unnoticed between runs.
options.numbers: As in C.
options.doc_edit: §24.1: the edge run is named as what checks the write budget; the cost table is recomputed from it.
options.build_change: As C, without the reads check in check_all.

recommendation.rationale: §24.1 calls its budget 'the design constraint, not an estimate made afterwards', yet it is measured on the wrong machine and ignores the free plan's hard cap of 5 million reads a day, which the target-list rebuild alone can exhaust at a few hundred islands (G21). Validation already needs the $5 paid plan (F47), so an edge run before soft launch costs only the deploy work and replaces local guesses with billed writes and real isolate CPU. Reads cost a thousandth of a write per row, so D is defensible, but only a checked reads budget catches periodic jobs whose cost grows with the number of islands rather than with play.

quotes.text: Budget: about 100 to 200 kilobytes and five writes per active player per day. That is the design constraint, not an estimate made afterwards (24.4).
The paid plan is $5 a month and includes 25 billion row reads and 50 million row writes — several times what a million players generate [199]
the free plan allows 5 million row reads and 100,000 row writes a day with 5 GB storage
a third of monthly players play on a given day

G33.also_needed: For B or C, the rows-read budget figure itself (1,500 per player-day fits the free plan at 10,000 monthly players, and 2,500 fits the paid plan's allowance at 1,000,000). For C or D, a Cloudflare account on the $5 Workers plan.

F51.question: What keeps a realm's edge open to land on, so that a Keeper cannot funnel every crew through one tile?
F51.why_it_matters: §5.4 makes open landing a pillar ('Defenders can't choose where raiders come from'), but the only edge rule in §6.1 protects the last route, not the edge. A realm ringed with blocking terrain and one gap publishes today, and its gap is the landing every crew must take, guarded by whatever stands beside it. That is the 'one guarded gate' §5.4 says the game does not have, and it changes what the hold rates in §13.2 measure.
F51.today: sim/src/island.rs check() requires one open edge tile (LandingBlocked) and a walkable route from some open edge tile to the Vault (Sealed). Island::landings() lists the open edge tiles; the simulation drops a landing anywhere else and verify_on refuses a heist that never lands. Nothing counts how many edge tiles are open.

options.label: No blocking terrain on the edge
options.means: No blocking feature and no Crystal Wall may stand on an edge tile, so every edge tile of a realm is a landing.
options.consequences: Landing is fully open, as §5.4 describes. A Keeper defends the edge only with what does not block: tall grass, fog, light, wards on open ground, guards and laws. 'Cliffs … along every edge' in §5.4's own reasoning has to go or become inland.
options.numbers: Every edge tile open: 36 at realm level 1 (10 by 10) up to 52 at level 5 (14 by 14), 4 × side − 4.
options.doc_edit: §5.4 'Landing' row: add 'No blocking terrain or Crystal Wall stands on an edge tile.' §6.1: the same rule beside the route rule.
options.build_change: island.rs check(): a new Problem, EdgeClosed, for any blocking feature or Crystal Wall on an edge tile; the builder shows it.

options.label: At least half of each side open
options.means: Each of a realm's four sides keeps at least half of its tiles open to land on, counting Crystal Walls as closed.
options.consequences: Cliffs and walls along the edge stay a tool, as §5.4's 'cliffs, tall grass, lantern light and laws along every edge' wants, but no side can be sealed and no single tile can become the gate. A Keeper still shapes where landing is easy.
options.numbers: At realm level 1 each side of 10 keeps 5 open, so at least 16 landings (a corner counts on both its sides); at level 5 each side of 14 keeps 7, at least 24.
options.doc_edit: §5.4 'Landing' row: add 'Each side of a realm keeps at least half its edge tiles open to land on.' §6.1: cite it beside the route rule.
options.build_change: island.rs check(): a new Problem, EdgeClosed, when any side has fewer than half its tiles open, with every Crystal Wall standing.

options.label: Keep the build's rule
options.means: One open edge tile and a route from some open edge tile to the Vault, which is all §6.1 asks.
options.consequences: A Keeper may wall the whole edge but one tile and choose where every crew lands. §5.4's 'Why open landing' then describes something the rules do not guarantee.
options.numbers: As few as 1 landing tile at any realm level.
options.doc_edit: §5.4 'Why open landing': say the edge is open unless the Keeper closes it, and that a realm may have one gate.
options.build_change: None.

recommendation.rationale: It is the smallest rule that makes §5.4's promise true: no side sealed and no single gate, while cliffs along the edge, which §5.4 names as defence, stay possible. A removes a tool the document wants; C contradicts the section's own reason for open landing.

quotes.text: Defenders can't choose where raiders come from; they can only make every edge a puzzle.
cliffs, tall grass, lantern light and laws along every edge
not one guarded gate
terrain can lengthen routes but never close the last route from the edges to the Heart

F51.also_needed: Whether a climbable cliff counts as open for landing; the build treats only walkable tiles as landings.

F52.question: Does a Lantern Glare's reach stretch with the alarm's, so Whispers makes it realm-wide again, or is it a fixed 4 m?
F52.why_it_matters: F33's answer made the Glare a local alarm, 4 m, and its build change took the alarm's reach, which Whispers sets to the whole universe. The defensive weave picks Whispers often, so on the harness two Glares still hold realm 3 at 91.5%, the switch F33 set out to remove. The brief's figures for F33's answer (68.2% and 75.2%) were measured with a fixed 4 m.
F52.today: sim/src/lib.rs spread_reach() is SPREAD_METRES (4) scaled by the sheet's AlarmRange; the Glare's reveal and the alarm spread both use it. tools/heist_harness/sim.py does the same (SPREAD_METRES * sheet.factor('alarm_range')). test_the_decided_glare_still_outweighs_a_realm_where_whispers_stretches_it pins 91.5% against 37.0%.

options.label: A fixed 4 m
options.means: The Glare shows the crew to the guards within 4 m of it, whatever the realm's alarm range. Whispers still carries a raised alarm to every guard in the universe, as its sheet says, but does not stretch the Glare.
options.consequences: F33's answer does what its figures said: one Glare is one strong pick among the kinds, not a switch. Whispers stays exactly what its Tier I cell says it is, an alarm law.
options.numbers: Harness, realm 3, two posts, defensive laws, competent crew, n=200: no wards 39.0%, one Glare 65.5%, two 72.5% (the brief measured 68.2% and 75.2% at n=400); six Snares and Wells 37.0%.
options.doc_edit: §10.3 Glare: 'Shows the crew to every guard within 4 m of it for 5 seconds (8 m from alarm level 4, 12.17) and blinds the crew for 2', adding 'a fixed reach, which laws that widen the alarm do not change'.
options.build_change: sim/src/lib.rs: the Glare's reveal uses SPREAD_METRES unscaled (keep spread_reach() for the alarm). tools/heist_harness/sim.py likewise; re-pin F52's test to the fixed reach.

options.label: Stretch with the alarm (the build)
options.means: The Glare reaches as far as the realm's alarm: 4 m, or the whole universe under Whispers.
options.consequences: A Whispers realm's Glare is realm-wide again, so two Glares and Whispers hold realm 3 near 90%. §5.2's budget has to be re-measured over kits with that case in, and Whispers becomes a much stronger defensive pick than its sheet reads.
options.numbers: Harness as A: two Glares 91.5% against six Snares and Wells' 37.0%.
options.doc_edit: §10.3 Glare: 'within the alarm's reach of it (4 m; the whole universe under Whispers)'.
options.build_change: None: this is what the build does.

recommendation.rationale: F33 was answered to stop one ward kind from deciding a realm; B brings that back through a law whose own sheet only talks about the alarm. A is what the brief's figures described.

quotes.text: Shows the crew to every guard in the realm for 5 seconds and blinds them for 2
Alarm spreads by distance, not everywhere at once: guards within four metres start investigating half a second later
When one guard raises the alarm, every guard in the universe hears it.

F52.also_needed: Whether the 8 m reach from alarm level 4 applies to the Glare, which the simulation does not build for the alarm either.

F53.question: B(V)'s base: 5,000, the every-day check with the fee an attempt keeps counted, or 4,600, the figure F36's answer named, with the fee left out of the check?
F53.why_it_matters: The base is the one dial on the raid faucet. F36's answer chose the rule (every day) and quoted its value before F39's fee was in the attempt; with the fee in, each day priced with that day's fee, the rule gives 5,000. Every haul, fee and cap moves with it: B(3) is 11,250 at 5,000 and 10,350 at 4,600.
F53.today: tools/design_facts.py HAUL_BASE = 5000, listed behind the document under F36; server/src/facts.json carries it. tools/economy_model/raidworth.py levels() prices each day's attempt with that day's fee (attempt_value() takes the fee off when Config.entry_fee is on) and binds each Vault level on its worst day; rerun.settle() ships smallest_passing_base(first_day_only=False).

options.label: 5,000: the rule, with the fee counted (the build)
options.means: The base is the smallest hundred at which an average attempt, less the fee it keeps, pays at least what the crew would have produced at home, on every day at every Vault level.
options.consequences: Hauls are 8.7% larger than at 4,600; the check and the fee agree, so no Vault level has a day on which raiding is the worse choice.
options.numbers: Every day with the fee: 5,000 (4,900 fails). Without the fee: 4,600. On the day each level arrives: 3,100. Birth rule: 1.3455 at both edges either way.
options.doc_edit: §9.6: 'B(V), the base — 5,000 × 1.5^(V−1)', and in 'What a raid must be worth': 'an average attempt, less the entry fee it keeps, pays at least …, on every day at a level'.
options.build_change: None: this is what the build does.

options.label: 4,600: the figure named, fee outside the check
options.means: The base is 4,600, and the check prices an attempt without its fee.
options.consequences: On some days an attempt, after its fee, pays a little less than staying home, the case §9.6's sentence says players skip.
options.numbers: At 4,600 with the fee counted the check fails; without it it passes on every day.
options.build_change: tools/design_facts.py HAUL_BASE = 4600 and facts.json regenerated; raidworth.attempt_value() leaves the fee out; the server tests re-pinned (B(3) 10,350, fee 207).

recommendation.rationale: The owner chose the rule, and the rule is about whether a raid is worth making; a fee the raid costs belongs in that sum.

quotes.text: at every Vault level, an average attempt pays at least what the same characters would have produced working over the heist and its rest
A crew on a heist does not work (5.8), and a raid that pays less than staying home is a raid players skip.

F54.why_it_matters: F37's answer made the launch 24 the non-raider's ceiling and Keeper 12 the first level that needs heists. Built, the plateau lands a hair below the next level, which reads as a bug, not a design.
F54.today: tools/economy_model: a never-raids player reaches Keeper 10 on day 82 and holds 2,223.5 of 2,230; test_finding_a_player_who_never_raids_stops_levelling pins it.

options.label: Show it as a gate
options.means: Nothing changes in the rules; the client shows the bar as waiting on the Spire (a gate), not as nearly full.
options.consequences: The ceiling F37 chose holds exactly; the near miss is a display question.
options.numbers: Keeper 10 from day 82; launch 24 by day 76.
options.doc_edit: §14.4: 'a player who never raids reaches Keeper 10 and the launch 24; its bar then waits on the Spire, which needs heists'.

options.label: Exactly one more level

G41.question: How much of the game should a player with no network be steered into: is offline the normal path, as §24.12 says, or the exception?
G41.why_it_matters: §24.12 builds the game for offline play first. That is what makes a heist on a train possible, but every heist played offline is shown as confirming and can come to nothing if its lease expired or its result does not reproduce. Most games of this kind stay online. How strongly the phone steers players online decides what the client asks for, what it shows while offline, and what §24.12 should say.
G41.today: The machinery is built: a lease from the server, play on the phone, the outbox (client/data/outbox.gd) keeping a replay until the server has it, validation and a grant (server/src/service.mjs), and a result shown as confirming until then (client/scripts/result_screen.gd). A heist started offline plays the fixture realm. Nothing keeps leases in stock, nothing recommends going online, and the outbox sends only when the next heist is submitted.

options.label: Online only
options.means: A heist needs a connection to start and to submit. With no network the Heist button says so and waits.
options.consequences: The simplest to build and to explain, and nothing is ever shown as confirming. A player underground cannot play.
options.numbers: None.
options.doc_edit: §24.12: replace its opening with online only, and drop the Play and Queue stages' offline cases.
options.build_change: The heist screen refuses to start offline; the outbox stays for a dropped submission.

options.label: Offline as the normal path (§24.12 as written)
options.means: The phone keeps leases and plays as if offline were ordinary; results confirm whenever the network returns.
options.consequences: The widest play, and the most results that wait or come to nothing, shown to players as a normal state.
options.numbers: A lease lasts a day (LEASE_MS, service.mjs:44), with one grace submission.
options.doc_edit: None.
options.build_change: A lease stock, the outbox sending on reconnect.

options.label: Online first, offline the exception
options.means: Online is the rule and is recommended heavily. While online the phone keeps a small stock of leases. Starting a heist offline shows a prompt recommending going online first, and the player may carry on. Hauls stay confirming until the server confirms them, and the outbox sends by itself on reconnecting, with a banner saying so.
options.consequences: Players are steered to the path where nothing waits, and a heist on a train still works. A little more to build than A.
options.numbers: A stock of three leases, refreshed while online; each lasts a day.
options.doc_edit: §24.12: its opening says online is the normal path and offline the exception, and names the stock, the prompt and the confirming states.
options.build_change: A lease stock in the heist repository, the offline prompt on the heist screen, the outbox flushed on reconnect with a banner.

recommendation.rationale: It keeps §24.12's safety for the train and the lift while steering players to the path where nothing is left confirming, as games of this kind do.

quotes.text: Offline is the normal path, not an edge case, and the rules below are architecture rather than polish.
